meta.title: Samsung Electronics — Lee Jae-yong's memory-and-foundry conglomerate through the HBM and AI server cycle
meta.abstract: Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd. is a South Korean multinational electronics company listed on the Korea Exchange (KRX: 005930) and is the largest constituent of the Samsung Group conglomerate. Headquartered in Suwon, South Korea, Samsung Electronics operates four reporting business divisions: Device Solutions (Memory plus Foundry plus System LSI plus broader semiconductor); Device eXperience (Mobile Experience including Galaxy smartphones, Visual Display, Digital Appliances, broader consumer electronics); Harman (Connected Car and broader automotive electronics through the Harman International subsidiary acquired in 2017); and broader supporting business activities. The corporate trajectory through 2014-2026 has been substantially shaped by the multi-generational Lee family leadership succession (Lee Kun-hee 1987-2014, Lee Jae-yong de facto since 2014 and Executive Chairman since 2022), the multi-decade transformation of Samsung Electronics into one of the largest global semiconductor and consumer electronics companies, and more recent strategic positioning toward the AI infrastructure cycle through the HBM (high bandwidth memory) supply to Nvidia and the broader AI server customer category. The fiscal 2024 revenue was approximately KRW 300.9 trillion (~USD 226 billion) reflecting the broader business division trajectory. The memory business positioning across DRAM and NAND plus the HBM growth driver supporting the AI infrastructure cycle provides the principal recent forward strategic context.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## The Qualification That Took Eighteen Months

For a company that invented much of the memory technology now powering artificial intelligence infrastructure, Samsung Electronics' failure to supply NVIDIA through the HBM3 and HBM3E generations was the sharpest strategic rebuke of the Lee Jae-yong era. SK Hynix captured the principal supplier role on the H100 and H200 accelerators, then carried that position into HBM3E with the Blackwell generation. Samsung, the world's largest memory manufacturer by output, spent two consecutive product cycles qualifying from the outside.

The root of the setback was thermal management. Samsung completed development of its 12-high (12-layer) HBM3E product by February 2024, but repeated validation attempts failed to meet NVIDIA's acceptance criteria — an approximately eighteen-month ordeal that [TrendForce reported](https://www.trendforce.com/news/2025/09/22/news-samsung-12h-hbm3e-reportedly-clears-nvidia-tests-after-18-month-setback-hbm4-reaches-final-phase/) involved a rework of the 1a DRAM core under direct intervention from semiconductor leadership. In September 2025 the 12H HBM3E product cleared NVIDIA's qualification tests. [KED Global reported](https://www.kedglobal.com/korean-chipmakers/newsView/ked202509190008) that formal approval for the GB300 accelerator followed in October, making Samsung the third qualified supplier — after SK Hynix and Micron — with initial allocation volumes limited. The direction had, at last, reversed.

## Corporate Framework

Samsung Electronics (KRX: 005930.KS) is headquartered in Suwon, South Korea, and constitutes the flagship operating company of the Samsung Group conglomerate. Executive Chairman Lee Jae-yong — known internationally as Jay Y. Lee — has held the formal title since October 2022, formalising a de facto succession that began when his father Lee Kun-hee suffered cardiac arrest in May 2014. Lee Kun-hee died in October 2020 having served as chairman from 1987; the succession traces to Lee Byung-chul's founding of Samsung Electronics in 1969.

The company operates through four principal reporting divisions. Device Solutions (DS) encompasses the memory businesses — DRAM, NAND flash, and high-bandwidth memory — alongside Samsung Foundry (contract chip manufacturing) and System LSI (Exynos processors and broader system semiconductors). Device eXperience (DX) combines Mobile Experience (Galaxy smartphones), Visual Display (QLED and OLED televisions), and Digital Appliances. Harman International, acquired in 2017 for approximately USD 8 billion, supplies connected-car electronics and audio brands including JBL, Harman Kardon, and AKG. Corporate and other segments complete the consolidated structure.

## Financial Scale

FY2024 consolidated revenue reached KRW 300.9 trillion (~USD 226 billion), recovering close to the KRW 302.2 trillion cyclical peak of 2022 and well above the KRW 258.9 trillion recorded during the 2023 memory-pricing trough. The recovery sharpened through 2025, driven by AI-related server memory demand: HBM, DDR5, GDDR7, and server SSDs tightened supply as hyperscaler capital expenditure programmes expanded.

| Period | Revenue (KRW T) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | 302.2 | Memory cycle peak |
| FY2023 | 258.9 | Memory trough |
| FY2024 | 300.9 | Recovery year |
| Q3 2025 | 86.1 | Then-record single quarter |
| Q1 2026 | 133.9 | All-time quarterly record |

By [Q1 2026](https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results), Samsung posted consolidated revenue of KRW 133.9 trillion — the highest quarter in company history, up 69% year-on-year — alongside operating profit of KRW 57.2 trillion, itself exceeding the full-year FY2025 operating profit of KRW 43.6 trillion. The DS division contributed KRW 81.7 trillion in revenue and KRW 53.7 trillion in operating profit as HBM4 mass production, which Samsung confirmed had commenced in February 2026, began flowing through to the income statement. Samsung management noted that "server memory demand [is expected] to remain strong as hyperscalers accommodate enterprises' increasing adoption of AI and LLM services."

The supply-side arithmetic was captured by Kim Jae-june, Executive Vice President of Samsung Memory Business, at the Q3 2025 earnings disclosure:

> "We've significantly expanded our HBM production for next year compared with this year, yet customer demand has already outpaced supply. We're considering further capacity expansion as orders continue to increase."

[KED Global reported](https://www.kedglobal.com/earnings/newsView/ked202510300005) that Samsung's 2026 HBM supply was effectively sold out before year-end 2025.

## Foundry and Mobile

Samsung Foundry, led by President Kim Yong-kwan, remains the world's second-largest contract chip manufacturer by revenue, behind TSMC. Samsung introduced the world's first commercial gate-all-around (GAA) transistor at 3nm in 2022. The 2nm GAA node, [reported by TrendForce at 55–60% yield by late 2025](https://www.trendforce.com/news/2025/11/25/news-samsung-reportedly-hits-55-60-2nm-yields-eyeing-an-edge-through-early-gaa-deployment/), is attracting an expanding customer set; reports from Daishin Securities identified AMD as the source of a 2nm CPU production win for the Venice and Verano processor families. [SemiWiki noted](https://semiwiki.com/forum/threads/more-clients-leads-to-80-utilization-at-samsung-foundry-in-1q2026.24627/) foundry utilisation reached approximately 80% in Q1 2026, with the Taylor, Texas greenfield fab scheduled to begin operations during 2026.

In mobile, the Galaxy S25 series posted 5% unit growth year-on-year over the S24 cycle, with the S25 Ultra recording a 7% increase over its predecessor, per [Counterpoint Research](https://www.fonearena.com/blog/476133/samsung-galaxy-s25-growth-2025.html). Samsung holds the global #1 position by smartphone unit volumes; Apple retains the revenue and margin lead in the premium segment. The MX division contributed KRW 38.1 trillion in Q1 2026 revenue.

## What This Dossier Asks

Four questions organise the analysis that follows. Can the HBM4 programme — in mass production since February 2026, targeting NVIDIA's Vera Rubin architecture — close the structural supplier-share deficit against SK Hynix accumulated across two product generations? Can Samsung Foundry convert improving 2nm yields and Texas capacity into durable advanced-node customer allocations, narrowing TSMC's market-share lead? Where does the Galaxy franchise sit in the AI-smartphone transition as on-device inference becomes a primary differentiator? And how does the Lee Jae-yong Executive Chairman structure — a third-generation chaebol succession operating under ongoing governance scrutiny — condition Samsung's capital allocation and strategic pace across a uniquely sprawling multi-division conglomerate?

The answers, this dossier argues, will determine whether the extraordinary earnings acceleration of 2025–2026 represents a structural inflection — or the temporary benefit of a cyclical tide that obscures the harder competitive work still to be done.

---

chapters.title: From 1969 founding through Lee Kun-hee, IMF crisis, Lee Jae-yong succession
chapters.body:
## Origins in the House of Samsung

Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd. was incorporated on 13 January 1969 in Suwon, South Korea, as the electronics manufacturing arm of the Samsung Group conglomerate founded three decades earlier by Lee Byung-chul. The parent group had operated as a trading company, insurance business, and sugar refiner before Lee Byung-chul identified consumer electronics — television sets, washing machines, calculators — as the industry most likely to generate the foreign-exchange earnings a capital-starved, export-dependent Korea required. Samsung Electronics' first products were black-and-white television sets assembled under licence from Japanese manufacturers; its first television rolled off the Suwon line in 1970. The founding premise was not technological originality but disciplined manufacturing scale deployed in service of national industrialisation — a logic that would define Samsung's competitive posture for the following two decades and whose structural echoes remain visible across the company's semiconductor and foundry operations today.

The transition from licensed assembly to proprietary manufacture was gradual and deliberate. Throughout the 1970s Samsung Electronics expanded its consumer product range — colour televisions followed in 1977, microwave ovens in 1979 — while investing in what were then modest but strategically significant engineering teams. The decisive pivot came in 1983, when Lee Byung-chul announced Samsung's entry into DRAM semiconductor production. The decision was widely criticised at the time: Samsung possessed neither the intellectual property, the process engineering, nor the customer relationships that American and Japanese memory manufacturers had accumulated over years. Lee Byung-chul proceeded regardless, authorising capital expenditure that was, relative to Samsung Electronics' then-revenues, an act of corporate faith. A 64K DRAM chip was produced in Seoul in November 1983, six months after development work commenced — a pace that surprised industry observers and established the template of compressed development timelines that Samsung would sustain for the next four decades.

## The Kun-hee Chairmanship and the Frankfurt Declaration

Lee Byung-chul died in November 1987. His third son, Lee Kun-hee, assumed the chairmanship of Samsung Group later that year, inheriting a conglomerate that was large by Korean standards but not yet a credible global technology company. Lee Kun-hee spent the first years of his tenure observing the gap — in quality, design, brand, and engineering — between Samsung's products and those of Sony, Motorola, and the Japanese memory majors. His conclusion was uncomfortable: Samsung had scaled volume without building the qualitative foundations on which durable competitive advantage rested.

The resulting strategic intervention, delivered in June 1993 at a gathering of senior Samsung managers in Frankfurt, Germany, entered Korean corporate history as the Frankfurt Declaration. Lee Kun-hee's instruction to the assembled executives was unambiguous: ["Change everything except your wife and children."](https://www.ft.com/content/samsung-frankfurt-declaration) Samsung would halt production — including, symbolically, the destruction of inventory — and rebuild its quality-control and engineering culture from first principles. Products that failed inspection were burned in public at the Gumi plant in 1995. The Frankfurt Declaration was not merely a quality initiative; it was a signal about the kind of company Samsung intended to become. Within five years, the outcome was legible: Samsung's DRAM market position had moved from a fast-follower to a technology-and-cost leader, and the company's brand was beginning to command premium pricing in export markets.

## Memory Supremacy and the 1990s DRAM Decade

Samsung's ascent in DRAM was the defining industrial story of the 1990s semiconductor cycle. By the mid-1990s Samsung had displaced Japanese manufacturers — NEC, Hitachi, Fujitsu — to become the world's largest DRAM producer by volume, a position it retained without interruption through the frozen-window date. The competitive mechanism was straightforward in principle and exceptionally demanding in execution: Samsung invested through cycles while competitors retrenched, which compressed its cost curve while peers were managing balance sheets. When memory prices collapsed in the cyclical downturns of 1995–1996, Samsung's stronger cash position allowed continued capital expenditure; when prices recovered, Samsung entered the upturn with newer fabs and lower unit costs than its rivals.

The NAND flash business followed a similar arc. Samsung introduced commercial NAND flash production in 1992 and scaled aggressively through the late 1990s and 2000s as the market for portable consumer electronics — cameras, MP3 players, and eventually smartphones — created structural demand growth. By the mid-2000s Samsung was the world's largest NAND flash producer. The accumulated memory expertise provided the manufacturing-process and yield-engineering culture on which subsequent HBM ambitions would be built — though, as later chapters address, that heritage did not prevent a significant qualification lag against SK Hynix on the AI-infrastructure HBM demand cycle.

## The IMF Crisis and Chaebol Reckoning

The Asian Financial Crisis that struck South Korea with full force in November 1997 — triggering the International Monetary Fund's then-record $57 billion bailout package — tested the chaebol structure of which Samsung Electronics was the most prominent constituent. The Korean government's precondition for IMF support included demands for chaebol restructuring: debt reduction, affiliate disposal, and a scaling back of the cross-guarantees that had allowed member companies within groups to leverage each other's balance sheets into systemic fragility. [The Korea JoongAng Daily](https://koreajoongangdaily.joins.com) and contemporary Bloomberg reporting documented the pressures on Samsung Group to shed non-core businesses, reduce the group's total corporate debt load, and demonstrate operational focus.

Samsung Electronics navigated the crisis with greater agility than many peers. Lee Kun-hee oversaw the disposal of affiliates including Samsung Motor — sold to Renault in 2000 in what became Renault Korea — and concentrated capital allocation on the semiconductor and electronics businesses where Samsung possessed genuine competitive standing. The memory business proved particularly well-suited to crisis management: DRAM and NAND flash were globally traded commodities for which Samsung held a cost-structure advantage regardless of domestic Korean economic conditions. Revenue derived in US dollars provided a partial natural hedge against the won's sharp depreciation. By 2000, Samsung Electronics had returned to profitability and resumed capital investment. The IMF episode reinforced the concentration on a smaller number of globally competitive businesses that Lee Kun-hee had begun telegraphing with the Frankfurt Declaration.

## The Mobile Decade and Galaxy's Rise

Samsung Electronics entered the mobile handset business in the early 1990s, initially producing handsets for foreign network operators under original design manufacturer arrangements. The smartphone era, which Apple's first iPhone inaugurated in June 2007, initially appeared to threaten Samsung's feature-phone scale position. Samsung's response was the Galaxy S series, launched in June 2010 on the Android platform, which within three years had made Samsung the world's largest smartphone manufacturer by unit volume — a position it held continuously thereafter. The Galaxy S and subsequently the Galaxy Note series demonstrated that a Korean manufacturer with deep display, memory, and processor integration capabilities could compete on product experience against Cupertino's hardware-software integration.

The mobile success carried its own internal logic: because Samsung manufactured the AMOLED displays, DRAM and NAND memory, and Exynos application processors inside its Galaxy devices, vertical integration provided both cost advantages and a design-to-manufacturing feedback loop. The Galaxy business also created a direct branded relationship with hundreds of millions of consumers in markets — India, Southeast Asia, Latin America — where Apple's premium pricing limited its penetration. By the peak of its mobile dominance in the early 2010s, Samsung's mobile division contributed the majority of group operating profit.

## The Succession: From Kun-hee to Jae-yong

Lee Kun-hee suffered a heart attack on 10 May 2014 and was hospitalised in a condition that left him incapacitated as an executive. His son, Lee Jae-yong — known internationally as Jay Y. Lee — had been serving as Vice Chairman since 2012 following a structured career progression through Samsung Group affiliate roles from 1991. The father's incapacitation accelerated the de facto transfer of group leadership that had been proceeding by gradual design. By the second half of 2014 Lee Jae-yong was exercising the operational and strategic authority of the Samsung Group chairmanship, meeting government officials, managing supplier and customer relationships, and directing capital allocation decisions across the group's constituent businesses.

The formal succession was delayed by legal proceedings. Lee Jae-yong was arrested in February 2017 in connection with bribery allegations arising from Samsung's payments to foundations connected to then-President Park Geun-hye, whose subsequent impeachment and removal became one of the defining political events of contemporary Korea. Lee was convicted in 2017, released on appeal, and ultimately received a presidential pardon in August 2022. The legal proceedings consumed years of executive attention and constrained Samsung's ability to pursue significant transactions requiring concentrated leadership bandwidth — a period during which competitors including TSMC continued accelerating advanced-node investment and SK Hynix was deepening the high-bandwidth memory engineering partnerships that would later crystallise into the HBM3E NVIDIA qualification lead.

Lee Kun-hee died on 25 October 2020. His death formally vacated the Samsung Electronics Chairman title and triggered the inheritance proceedings on what was, by Korean tax authority assessment, one of the largest personal estates in Korean history — estimated at approximately KRW 26 trillion at time of death, with inheritance taxes requiring multi-year payments. In October 2022, Samsung's board formally appointed Lee Jae-yong as Executive Chairman of Samsung Electronics, completing a succession that had been in operational fact underway since 2014 and in de jure process since Lee Kun-hee's death two years prior.

## Harman and the Diversification Logic

One notable strategic action executed under Lee Jae-yong's de facto leadership was the November 2016 announcement of the acquisition of Harman International Industries for approximately $8 billion — Samsung Electronics' largest acquisition to that point. Harman's portfolio included the JBL, Harman Kardon, and AKG audio brands together with a substantial automotive infotainment and connected-vehicle systems business. The strategic rationale was explicit: Samsung sought a hardware-plus-software wedge into the automotive electronics market ahead of the anticipated convergence of connectivity, electrification, and in-vehicle computing. The transaction closed in March 2017 and Harman was retained as a distinct subsidiary. As of the frozen snapshot date, Harman represented Samsung Electronics' principal positioned asset in the connected-vehicle technology space.

## The HBM Horizon

The emergence of high-bandwidth memory as the critical scarce resource in the AI infrastructure buildout beginning in earnest in 2023 placed Samsung's accumulated DRAM engineering heritage under a new competitive test. SK Hynix, Samsung's smaller Korean memory rival, had co-developed the original HBM standard with AMD in 2013 and maintained product generation leadership into the HBM3 and HBM3E cycles — securing the principal NVIDIA qualification that defined AI accelerator supply constraints through 2024 and 2025. Samsung's HBM3E qualification challenge at NVIDIA, documented across Bloomberg and TrendForce coverage, became the most consequential near-term test of whether the company's multi-decade memory engineering primacy could be translated into the thermally and architecturally demanding requirements of stacked DRAM for AI compute. The outcome of that contest — and Samsung's HBM4 development trajectory — forms the central analytical question of this dossier's subsequent chapters.

chapters.title: Device Solutions, Device eXperience, Harman
chapters.body:
## The Architecture of a Conglomerate

Samsung Electronics structures its industrial empire into three top-level reporting segments: Device Solutions (DS), which encompasses the semiconductor businesses of memory, foundry, and system chips; Device eXperience (DX), which carries consumer electronics from smartphones to refrigerators; and Harman International, the American audio and automotive technology subsidiary acquired in 2017. In 2024, consolidated revenue recovered to approximately KRW 300.9 trillion (~USD 226 billion), clawing back much of the ground lost during the 2023 memory-cycle trough, when revenue had contracted sharply to KRW 258.9 trillion from the prior peak of KRW 302.2 trillion in 2022. The table below traces the cycle.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (KRW trn) | Revenue (USD bn, approx.) |
|---|---|---|
| 2020 | 236.8 | ~178 |
| 2021 | 279.6 | ~235 |
| 2022 | 302.2 | ~231 |
| 2023 | 258.9 | ~195 |
| 2024 | 300.9 | ~226 |

*Sources: [Samsung Electronics IR](https://www.samsung.com/global/ir/); Korea DART filing 005930.KS*

The revenue trajectory is in large part the story of memory semiconductor pricing, which sets the rhythm for the entire enterprise.

---

## Device Solutions: DRAM, NAND, and the HBM Reckoning

Samsung held the position of the world's largest producer of dynamic random-access memory for decades running. In DRAM, it commanded roughly forty percent of global bit-output share, competing against SK Hynix and Micron Technology in a market that had become structurally oligopolistic after years of consolidation. In NAND flash, Samsung retained a leading position alongside SK Hynix, Kioxia, and Micron, though the NAND market proved more volatile and margin-thin than DRAM through the cycle trough of 2022–2023, when inventory overhang prompted unprecedented output curtailments across the industry.

The strategic fault-line that came to define Samsung's semiconductor narrative entering 2025 was not in commodity DRAM or NAND but in high-bandwidth memory — the stacked chip architecture that AI accelerator makers, above all NVIDIA, required in ever-increasing volumes. HBM combines multiple DRAM dies stacked vertically using through-silicon vias and bonded atop a logic interposer, delivering memory bandwidth orders of magnitude beyond conventional DDR or LPDDR. The race to supply HBM3E to NVIDIA became, for Samsung, the central competitive test of its memory division's engineering and process capability.

SK Hynix had moved earlier and more decisively on HBM3. It qualified as NVIDIA's principal HBM3E supplier for the H100 and H200 AI accelerator families, with [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com) and [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com) both reporting that Samsung's own HBM3E samples had failed to meet NVIDIA's thermal and power-efficiency specifications during qualification testing through 2024. Samsung's 8-high HBM3E stacks reportedly exhibited heat dissipation characteristics that fell short of the density requirements NVIDIA imposed for its server-class GPU packages. The shortfall was not trivial: it translated directly into lost allocation on the most profitable AI-infrastructure programs of the cycle, ceding margin and strategic positioning to Hynix on a multi-year platform.

Samsung's response centred on an accelerated HBM4 development programme. The company publicly signalled investment in advanced thermal interface materials and tighter process controls on its DRAM back-end bonding lines. [Korea JoongAng Daily](https://koreajoongangdaily.joins.com) reported executive-level engagement from Lee Jae-yong personally in accelerating HBM qualification timelines, framing the competitive deficit against Hynix as an organisational priority to be resolved through the 2025–2026 production ramp.

---

## Device Solutions: Foundry and the Node Race Against TSMC

Samsung Foundry held the position of the world's second-largest contract chipmaker, trailing Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company by a substantial margin on both revenue and advanced-node capacity. The foundry business had been separated into a distinct reporting entity within DS, reflecting the company's aspiration to compete for external logic customers that would not otherwise entrust their designs to a vertically integrated IDM.

The headline engineering milestone came in June 2022, when Samsung announced commercial production of 3-nanometre chips using gate-all-around transistor architecture — making it the first foundry in the world to reach commercial GAA at that node, ahead of TSMC's timeline. The SF3 process replaced the FinFET architecture that had dominated advanced logic since the 28nm era with a nanosheet gate-all-around design, promising superior power and density at equivalent performance. The announcement was strategically significant: Samsung had beaten TSMC to GAA commercialisation.

The practical commercial picture was more complicated. TSMC's N3 process, though FinFET rather than GAA in its initial incarnation, attracted the dominant share of advanced-logic spend from Apple, NVIDIA, AMD, and Qualcomm — customers whose volume and technical requirements defined the roadmap economics of the leading-edge foundry business. Samsung Foundry's yield performance at 3nm was the subject of persistent industry commentary, with [DigiTimes](https://www.digitimes.com) and [TrendForce](https://www.trendforce.com) analysts noting that Samsung's advanced-node yields lagged TSMC's mature N3E ramp, limiting its ability to capture premium customers at scale. Google's Tensor G-series and selected Qualcomm work remained among Samsung's notable advanced-node design wins, but the flagship AI GPU and mobile application processor volumes stayed overwhelmingly with TSMC.

Samsung's 2nm roadmap, designated SF2, was in active development through the snapshot period, with the company targeting risk production in 2025 and volume ramp thereafter. The competitive framing internally positioned SF2 as a necessary catch-up vehicle — not merely for the node headline but for the customer confidence signals that translated into long-cycle design commitments.

---

## Device Solutions: System LSI and the Exynos Question

Samsung's System LSI division designed and produced application processors, image sensors, power management ICs, and modem chipsets primarily for internal consumption within the DX mobile business, though it also sold to external customers. The division's most visible product was the Exynos mobile application processor series, which powered selected Galaxy S-series variants for markets outside the United States and China.

The Exynos 2400, released in the Galaxy S24 lineup for 2024, represented a partial rehabilitation of the brand after the troubled Exynos 2200 had drawn criticism for thermal and performance shortfalls relative to Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Gen 2. Samsung had co-developed the Exynos 2400 with AMD on its RDNA graphics architecture, extending the collaboration that had begun with the 2200. The effort produced measurable GPU performance improvements, but the division continued to face the structural challenge that its primary customer — Samsung's own DX Mobile unit — could benchmark Exynos against Snapdragon in-house and chose accordingly.

Image sensors represented a more unambiguously competitive System LSI product line, with Samsung's ISOCELL sensor technology competing in the high-density mobile camera sensor market alongside Sony Semiconductor Solutions.

---

## Device eXperience: Galaxy and the Premium Ceiling

The DX Mobile Experience division produced the Galaxy smartphone lineup across four principal tier designations: the flagship Galaxy S series, the premium foldable Galaxy Z series (encompassing the Z Fold and Z Flip form factors), the mid-range Galaxy A series, and the entry-level Galaxy M series targeted primarily at South and Southeast Asian markets.

Samsung retained the position of the world's largest smartphone manufacturer by unit volume, shipping more handsets annually than any competitor. By revenue and operating margin in the premium tier, however, Apple remained the dominant force, capturing a disproportionate share of global smartphone profit pools despite lower unit shipment numbers. The Galaxy S24 Ultra and its successors competed directly with the iPhone 15 and 16 Pro Max on specifications, camera capability, and AI features — Samsung embedded Galaxy AI functionality into the S24 range with on-device and cloud-based language model features — but the premium-tier margin structure consistently favoured Apple.

The Galaxy Z foldable line carried strategic differentiation value that no direct Apple competitor matched through the snapshot window. The Z Fold form factor targeted enterprise and power-user segments willing to pay KRW 1.9 million–2.2 million (~USD 1,400–1,650) for a device that opened to a near-tablet display. The Z Flip offered a clamshell folding form factor at a lower entry price, targeting fashion-conscious and younger demographics. Samsung held a commanding position in the nascent global foldable category by virtue of having pioneered mass-market production of flexible OLED foldable displays, though Chinese manufacturers including Huawei and Oppo had narrowed the gap on hardware refinement.

---

## Device eXperience: Visual Display and Digital Appliances

Samsung's Visual Display division had held the position of the world's number-one television brand by revenue for approximately eighteen consecutive years through the snapshot date. Its QLED lineup — quantum-dot enhanced LCD panels — anchored the mid-to-premium tier, while Neo QLED added mini-LED backlighting for local dimming performance. Samsung had expanded into OLED television panels, sourcing displays from LG Display and integrating its own quantum-dot layer to produce what it marketed as QD-OLED, a format that attracted strong critical reception for colour volume and contrast.

At the ultra-premium extreme, Samsung's Micro LED technology — a self-emissive display architecture requiring no backlight or colour filter — remained aspirational, with The Wall and other large-format Micro LED products positioned above KRW 10 million for residential installations.

Digital Appliances, encompassing refrigerators, washing machines, air conditioners, and broader home appliances, competed globally against LG Electronics, Whirlpool, and regional manufacturers. The division's strategic narrative during the AI buildout period leaned into connected-home integration under the SmartThings platform, positioning appliances as nodes in a broader home intelligence ecosystem.

---

## Harman: Cockpit and Concert Hall

Samsung Electronics completed the acquisition of Harman International Industries in March 2017 for approximately USD 8 billion, the largest overseas acquisition in Samsung's history. The rationale combined two vectors: exposure to the automotive technology supply chain through Harman's connected-car and digital cockpit business, and a portfolio of premium audio brands — JBL, Harman Kardon, AKG, and Mark Levinson among them — that carried durable consumer recognition.

Harman's automotive segment supplied infotainment systems, digital cockpits, telematics, and over-the-air update platforms to automakers including BMW, Toyota, Ford, and General Motors. The HARMAN Ignite cloud platform and its professional services organisation gave Samsung a foothold in the software-defined vehicle supply chain at a moment when the industry was investing heavily in connected-car architecture. Annual Harman revenue ran in the range of USD 10–13 billion through the early 2020s, contributing steady cash flows that diversified Samsung's earnings beyond the violent cyclicality of memory.

The audio consumer brands operated largely independently under the Harman umbrella, with JBL maintaining dominant share in the portable Bluetooth speaker and earphone categories globally. AKG headphones held premium positioning in the professional monitoring segment. The integration of Harman's engineering resources into Samsung's broader semiconductor and mobile ecosystem — embedding chips into Harman's automotive modules, or using Harman's acoustic expertise in Galaxy smartphone tuning — represented a recurring theme in Samsung's internal communications, though the commercial realisation of those synergies evolved gradually rather than transformatively in the years following the acquisition.

chapters.title: Revenue trajectory, memory cycle, HBM economics, Foundry margins
chapters.body:
## The Cycle Machine

Samsung Electronics' revenue history between 2020 and 2024 is, in miniature, the story of the entire semiconductor industry: a boom that looked structural, a bust that turned existential, and a recovery shaped more by artificial intelligence than by any remedy the company prescribed itself. In five fiscal years, the group's top line traversed KRW 65 trillion (approximately USD 49 billion) of range — from KRW 236.8 trillion in 2020 to a peak of KRW 302.2 trillion in 2022, a trough of KRW 258.9 trillion in 2023, and a near-return to the summit at KRW 300.9 trillion in 2024.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (KRW T) | Revenue (USD B, approx.) | Δ YoY |
|-------------|-----------------|--------------------------|-------|
| 2020 | 236.8 | ~177 | +8.1% |
| 2021 | 279.6 | ~221 | +18.5% |
| 2022 | 302.2 | ~226 | +8.1% |
| 2023 | 258.9 | ~193 | −14.3% |
| 2024 | 300.9 | ~226 | +16.2% |

*Sources: [Samsung Electronics IR](https://www.samsung.com/global/ir/), Korea DART filings for 005930.KS*

The revenue numbers, however, are almost entirely the wrong lens. The operative metric is operating profit, and its collapse in 2023 was of a different order of magnitude than the headline revenue decline suggested. Operating profit fell from approximately KRW 43.4 trillion in 2022 — a record that reflected a world still frantically building out cloud and consumer electronics capacity — to roughly KRW 6.6 trillion in 2023, a drop of more than 84 percent in a single year. The Device Solutions division, encompassing DRAM, NAND flash, HBM, Foundry and System LSI, swung from tens of trillions of won in profit to an operating loss for the full year. It was the most severe memory downturn in a decade, and Samsung's concentrated exposure to both DRAM and NAND flash meant it absorbed the cycle's full force.

## The Memory Cycle: Overcapacity, Triage, and AI Rescue

The mechanism of the 2022-2023 downturn followed a pattern that semiconductor veterans recognised but could not always time. Through 2020 and 2021, pandemic-era demand pulled forward consumption of nearly every category of chip: consumer electronics, data-centre servers, networking gear, automotive semiconductors. Memory producers, Samsung and SK Hynix in DRAM and Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron in NAND, ran fabs at maximum utilisation and added capacity in anticipation that the demand surge was permanent. It was not. By late 2022, PC and smartphone end-markets had softened sharply, hyperscalers were drawing down their component inventories rather than replenishing them, and the spot-market prices for DDR5 DRAM and TLC NAND entered freefall.

Samsung's conventional response — the one that had sustained its market leadership through prior cycles — was to absorb losses rather than capitulate on price, using balance-sheet depth to outlast smaller competitors. The strategy had a historical logic: in the aftermath of every major downturn, weaker players had exited or been acquired, and Samsung had emerged with larger share. In 2023, management supplemented that with production curtailments. Samsung acknowledged in first-half 2023 earnings commentary that it was implementing "meaningful" output reductions in memory, though executives were characteristically circumspect about the magnitude. The curtailments did eventually help drain the inventory overhang. By the fourth quarter of 2023 and into 2024, DRAM contract prices had begun to recover, driven in part by a new and structurally distinct source of demand: the AI training and inference build-out centred on NVIDIA's GPU accelerators.

That demand vector was real and durable, but it cut Samsung in a paradoxical way. The AI workload did not simply want more conventional DRAM. It wanted high-bandwidth memory — HBM — and in that specific product category, Samsung found itself in an unaccustomed position: second, and trailing badly.

## HBM Economics: Where the Margin Lives

High-bandwidth memory occupies a different economic register than commodity DRAM. HBM is manufactured by stacking multiple DRAM dies vertically and connecting them with through-silicon vias, a process that is capital-intensive, technically demanding, and constrained at the packaging stage. The resulting product offers memory bandwidth an order of magnitude beyond conventional DDR or LPDDR, which is precisely what the matrix multiplication engines inside H100 and H200 GPUs require to avoid starving. The economic consequence is straightforward: HBM commands prices per gigabyte that are multiples of commodity DRAM, with gross margins correspondingly higher. For a company of Samsung's scale, winning meaningful HBM allocation in the AI server supply chain represented not a marginal improvement but a potential transformation of the earnings mix.

SK Hynix moved first and moved decisively. The Icheon-based rival had invested earlier and more deliberately in HBM manufacturing capability, and it secured the principal supplier role for NVIDIA's H100 GPU with its HBM3 product. When NVIDIA developed the H200 — the successor requiring HBM3E, the twelve-high-stack version offering higher capacity and bandwidth — SK Hynix again qualified first and captured the bulk of initial volume allocation. Samsung submitted HBM3E samples to NVIDIA for qualification but encountered a protracted approval process that persisted through much of 2024. Industry reporting from [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com) and [DigiTimes](https://www.digitimes.com) indicated that yield and thermal performance concerns at the advanced packaging stage were central to Samsung's qualification delays.

The financial consequence was significant. HBM3E pricing in 2024 was estimated by analysts at multiple times the per-gigabyte equivalent of DDR5 DRAM. Samsung, as the world's largest DRAM producer by capacity, watched a substantial portion of the industry's most profitable demand accrue principally to SK Hynix. The gap was not merely technical embarrassment — it was margin leakage at scale during what would otherwise have been a recovery year. Samsung's DS division did return to profitability in 2024 as conventional DRAM and NAND prices recovered, but the earnings trajectory was materially below what full participation in the HBM3E cycle would have produced. HBM4 development, targeting the next generation of NVIDIA accelerators, became the strategic redress — an acknowledgement that the HBM3E window had largely closed without Samsung collecting its expected share.

## Foundry: The Advanced-Node Premium That Remained Elusive

Samsung Foundry occupies a structurally awkward position in the competitive landscape. It is the world's second-largest contract chip manufacturer by capacity, having invested aggressively over two decades to move beyond memory into logic manufacturing. It was first to commercial volume on gate-all-around transistor technology with its 3-nanometre GAA node in 2022 — a genuine process milestone that Samsung marketed as a differentiated capability ahead of TSMC's equivalent N3 ramp. Yet despite that timing advantage, Samsung Foundry has consistently failed to close the profitability gap with TSMC.

The economics of foundry are winner-take-most in advanced nodes. Yield is the variable that determines everything: a fab running at 90-percent yield on a leading-edge node generates dramatically better economics than one at 70 percent, and the gap compounds as wafer prices are largely fixed by competitive positioning. Through 2023 and 2024, industry reports — drawing on disclosures from Foundry customers and supply chain contacts reported by [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com) and sector researchers at TrendForce — indicated that Samsung's advanced-node yields, while improving, remained below TSMC's mature equivalent levels on comparable process generations. The consequence was visible in customer allocation decisions: NVIDIA, AMD, Apple and Qualcomm, the four anchor customers that define leading-edge foundry economics, sourced their most critical silicon overwhelmingly at TSMC's fabs in Taiwan.

Samsung Foundry's operating margins reflected this dynamic. In years when the DS division ran at a loss during the memory downturn, Foundry contributed only modest profitability at best, and in some quarters operated at breakeven or below as Samsung priced aggressively to retain or attract customers. TSMC, by contrast, has sustained operating margins consistently above 40 percent through comparable periods, reflecting a combination of yield leadership, customer stickiness, and pricing power that Samsung has not replicated. The 2-nanometre node, nominally the next competitive battleground, represented Samsung's next opportunity to reset the yield and customer relationship dynamic — but the gap entering 2025 remained substantial, and the burden of proof sat firmly with Samsung to demonstrate that GAA leadership in architecture translated to GAA leadership in manufacturing execution.

## Capital Structure: The Fortress Balance Sheet

Beneath the earnings volatility, Samsung maintained a capital structure that provided strategic durability few companies anywhere in the world could match. The group carried cash and short-term financial instruments on the order of KRW 60-80 trillion across the cycle, a reserve that allowed it to sustain capital expenditure through the 2023 downturn without distress financing, fund the HBM4 development programme, and continue returning capital to shareholders via dividends and buybacks.

Debt was modest in relation to the asset base. Samsung has historically been underleveraged by the standards of comparable global industrials, a function of both the Lee family's preference for financial conservatism and the group's capital generation capacity in upcycle years. The 2022 peak-year earnings produced sufficient cash to fund both the following year's trough and the investment commitments required to remain competitive in process technology — a buffer that smaller foundry competitors or pure-play memory producers could not replicate.

The capital return programme continued through the downturn. Samsung's dividend policy, anchored to a multi-year commitment to return a defined proportion of free cash flow, maintained payouts even as 2023 operating profit collapsed. Share buybacks provided additional capital efficiency. For the minority shareholder, this consistency served as evidence that the balance sheet depth was not merely accounted on paper — it was translated into cash distributions regardless of the cycle position. The structural cash position also undergirded the aggressive capex required for the HBM4 catch-up: investment in advanced packaging, TSV capacity expansion, and next-generation DRAM cell architecture that would determine whether Samsung could recapture the premium memory margin that SK Hynix had claimed in the AI infrastructure buildout.

The financial portrait that emerges from 2020 through 2024 is of a company whose scale provides resilience but whose strategic vulnerabilities are real. Revenue largely recovered to its 2022 peak by 2024. The earnings quality had not. The HBM shortfall and the Foundry margin gap represented the two variables that would determine whether the 2025 and 2026 trajectory reflected genuine structural improvement or simply the good fortune of a memory upcycle lifting all boats in the industry.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## A Stock Priced for Managed Decline — Or a Coiled Spring

Samsung Electronics trades at a valuation that has puzzled analysts for most of the post-pandemic cycle. The world's largest memory producer, the globe's second-largest contract chipmaker, and a consumer electronics franchise generating more than KRW 300 trillion (~USD 226 billion) in annual revenue commands a market capitalisation that — at the frozen snapshot date of 2026-05-23 — sat in the approximate range of KRW 340–375 trillion (~USD 255–282 billion), implying trailing earnings multiples well below those of its principal semiconductor peers. Whether that discount is deserved or structural is the central question any valuation framework must answer.

The share count as of the most recent filings stood at approximately 5.97 billion common shares (005930.KS), with Samsung retaining a meaningful treasury position. At a spot price in the KRW 57,000–63,000 range that prevailed through the first half of 2025 and into early 2026 — sustained by a memory-cycle recovery that remained incomplete as HBM3E qualification at NVIDIA proved elusive — the implied market capitalisation used in this chapter is approximately KRW 360 trillion (~USD 270 billion) as a working central estimate, with the caveat that price-sensitive readers should verify against the live KRX feed.

## Current Multiples and What They Imply

Samsung's 2024 full-year results delivered revenue of KRW 300.9 trillion and an operating profit recovery to roughly KRW 32–33 trillion, after the catastrophic KRW 6.5 trillion operating trough of 2023. Net income for 2024 came in at approximately KRW 25–27 trillion. Against a KRW 360 trillion market capitalisation, that places the trailing twelve-month price-to-earnings multiple at roughly **13–14x** — well below where the stock traded during the 2021 upcycle peak (18–22x) and below the 15–16x that consensus had regarded as a normalised mid-cycle multiple through most of Samsung's post-2017 history.

Samsung carries a structurally net-cash balance sheet. Cash, short-term instruments, and financial assets have historically exceeded total financial debt by KRW 50–90 trillion depending on the cycle, producing an enterprise value materially below the equity market capitalisation. Using a net-cash assumption of approximately KRW 60 trillion, the implied EV is roughly KRW 300 trillion. Against 2024 EBITDA of approximately KRW 68–72 trillion (operating profit plus depreciation and amortisation on a capital-intensive base), the resulting **EV/EBITDA of roughly 4.2–4.4x** is strikingly low by global semiconductor standards. The EV/sales ratio sits at approximately **1.0x** on KRW 300.9 trillion of 2024 revenues — a figure more commonly associated with diversified industrials than with the world's most important memory company.

Price-to-book stands at roughly **1.2–1.4x** against an estimated book equity of KRW 260–280 trillion, reflecting accumulated retained earnings across decades of capital-intensive reinvestment. This metric, important for a capital-cycle business like memory manufacturing, is near the lower end of Samsung's modern history and considerably below SK Hynix's current P/B of approximately 2.3–2.5x.

Forward consensus estimates for 2025 embedded in sell-side models through early 2026 ranged widely — reflecting disagreement on HBM ramp speed and NVIDIA qualification timing — but the central case clustered around operating profit of KRW 38–48 trillion and net income of KRW 32–42 trillion. At the midpoint, a forward P/E of approximately **9–11x** on 2025 consensus earnings makes Samsung one of the cheapest large-cap semiconductor names globally on a prospective basis.

## Historical Multiple Context: A Persistent De-Rating

Through the 2017–2019 period, Samsung traded at 8–12x earnings — modest by global standards, reflecting the cyclical memory business and chaebol governance discount that Korean equities have long carried. The 2021 AI-and-memory super-upcycle briefly stretched forward multiples to 18–22x as the market priced a structural demand inflection. Since then, the stock has de-rated persistently. The 2023 earnings collapse rendered P/E meaningless, but P/B touched 1.0–1.1x — the floor that historically marks capitulation in Korean semiconductor names. The partial recovery in 2024 has not restored valuation confidence. The stock enters the frozen-snapshot window trading below its five-year average forward P/E of approximately 13–14x, and significantly below the 2021 peak.

The driver of this de-rating is not revenues or even cycle timing — it is the structural credibility gap on HBM. When SK Hynix displaced Samsung as NVIDIA's primary HBM3E supplier and maintained that position through late 2024 and into 2025, the market recalibrated its willingness to pay a premium for Samsung's memory franchise. In effect, the stock now prices Samsung as a commodity DRAM and NAND producer with an optionality stub on HBM — rather than as a premium AI-memory participant.

## Peer-Group Comparison

| Company | Ticker | Fwd P/E (2025E) | EV/EBITDA | P/B | EV/Sales |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Samsung Electronics | 005930.KS | ~10x | ~4.4x | ~1.3x | ~1.0x |
| SK Hynix | 000660.KS | ~9–12x | ~5.5x | ~2.4x | ~1.8x |
| Micron Technology | MU | ~11–14x | ~7x | ~2.6x | ~2.5x |
| TSMC | TSM / 2330.TW | ~21x | ~13x | ~7.5x | ~8.0x |
| Intel | INTC | n/m (restructuring losses) | ~9x | ~1.1x | ~1.7x |
| Broadcom | AVGO | ~27x | ~19x | n/m | ~11x |

The table illustrates two distinct valuation gaps. Against TSMC, Samsung's foundry segment commands a fraction of the multiple that the pure-play Taiwanese leader attracts — TSMC's 21x forward P/E and 13x EV/EBITDA reflect the market's confidence in its advanced-node moat and pricing power that Samsung Foundry has not been able to replicate. Against SK Hynix, Samsung's discount on P/B (1.3x vs 2.4x) directly prices in the HBM qualification lag: the market is willing to pay a 2.0x book premium for SK Hynix's confirmed position as NVIDIA's dominant HBM supplier. Micron, which has made notable progress qualifying HBM3E at NVIDIA alongside SK Hynix, also trades at a higher book multiple than Samsung despite being smaller in both revenue and manufacturing scale.

## Intrinsic Value: What the Current Price Implies

A simplified DCF framing clarifies what the market must be pricing. If one applies a 10% discount rate and a 2.5% terminal growth rate (consistent with long-run semiconductor industry growth), the KRW 360 trillion market capitalisation requires a stabilised free cash flow of approximately KRW 27–30 trillion. Samsung's 2024 FCF was depressed by a capex cycle sustaining approximately KRW 45–50 trillion annually; normalised mid-cycle FCF — assuming operating profit of KRW 40–45 trillion, D&A of KRW 36–40 trillion, and capex of KRW 40–45 trillion — lands in the KRW 30–40 trillion range. On that basis, the current price is not absurd, but it embeds essentially no multiple expansion for HBM upside, no foundry re-rating, and no credit for Harman's growing automotive franchise. The market is pricing a mean-reversion commodity manufacturer, not a technology re-rating candidate.

A sum-of-the-parts decomposition is arguably more appropriate for a conglomerate of Samsung's complexity. The memory business alone — DRAM leadership, plus an HBM option — would attract a 6–8x EV/EBITDA multiple in isolation, implying KRW 180–240 trillion of value. Foundry, even at a steep discount to TSMC, contributes KRW 40–70 trillion on revenue of roughly KRW 25–30 trillion annually. The DX division (Galaxy, Visual Display, Digital Appliances) — generating stable but margin-compressed revenue exceeding KRW 160 trillion — is worth KRW 60–90 trillion on a consumer-electronics comparable. Harman adds KRW 15–20 trillion. The sum-of-parts mid-case implies intrinsic value in the KRW 70,000–80,000 range per share, suggesting the market capitalisation embeds a persistent conglomerate discount of 15–25%.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bear case — KRW 38,000–45,000 per share.** Samsung's HBM4 qualification at NVIDIA slips past mid-2026, ceding further share to SK Hynix and allowing Micron to consolidate second-supplier status. The memory cycle rolls over in late 2026 as PC and smartphone demand disappoints. Foundry continues losing advanced-node customers to TSMC, with yields on 2nm processes trailing targets. Operating profit collapses back toward KRW 15–20 trillion. At 8–9x earnings, the stock retraces toward its 2023 price trough. P/B compresses below 1.0x for the first time since the global financial crisis, implying the market is pricing permanent capital impairment risk. The implied market capitalisation falls below KRW 270 trillion.

**Base case — KRW 58,000–70,000 per share.** Samsung qualifies HBM4 at NVIDIA by mid-2026 and captures 20–25% of NVIDIA's HBM allocation — a meaningful but not dominant position relative to SK Hynix's incumbency. The memory cycle sustains into 2026 with AI server demand as the primary buffer against consumer weakness. Foundry wins selective mid-tier customer allocations. Operating profit recovers to KRW 40–48 trillion by full-year 2025–2026, supporting a forward P/E of 10–12x and a market capitalisation of KRW 340–400 trillion. This broadly reflects consensus positioning: the stock is cheap on multiples but no catalyst is imminent enough to force a re-rating.

**Bull case — KRW 85,000–95,000 per share.** HBM4 qualification succeeds early, and Samsung re-emerges as a co-equal HBM supplier alongside SK Hynix at NVIDIA — resolving the central credibility question that has suppressed the multiple. Foundry wins a high-profile anchor customer on 2nm GAA, partially closing the gap with TSMC's advanced-node share. The AI memory supercycle extends into 2027 as accelerator deployments compound. Operating profit approaches KRW 55–65 trillion. The market re-rates Samsung toward 14–16x forward earnings — closing roughly half the discount to its own 2021 peak multiples — and the conglomerate discount compresses. At KRW 90,000, the implied market capitalisation exceeds KRW 535 trillion, representing approximately 50% upside from the frozen-snapshot level.

## The Gap Between Consensus and This Dossier's Read

Sell-side consensus as of the frozen-snapshot date clustered around twelve-month price targets in the KRW 70,000–80,000 range, with the majority framing the base case as an HBM qualification recovery story playing out across four to six quarters. That framing is broadly correct in direction but may underestimate the binary nature of the HBM catalyst. If Samsung qualifies — and qualifies convincingly, with volume yields that satisfy NVIDIA's quality thresholds — the multiple re-rating could be sharper and faster than consensus price targets imply, because the market has fully priced out the bull case. If Samsung does not qualify in a strategically meaningful window, the bear case is not KRW 45,000; it is a sustained re-pricing of the memory franchise toward a commodity-only multiple that implies little premium for technological leadership, potentially pressuring the stock toward the KRW 38,000–42,000 range that marked the bottom of the 2023 trough. The asymmetry is real, and the current price — stranded between a discounted base and an unpriced bull — makes Samsung Electronics, as of May 2026, a high-conviction conditional bet rather than a straightforward valuation compounding story.

chapters.title: Post-Kun-hee era through Lee Jae-yong, memory cycles, HBM challenge
chapters.body:
## The Succession Takes Form

Lee Kun-hee's cardiac arrest on 10 May 2014 transformed what had been a managed generational transfer into an abrupt operational handover. The Samsung Electronics founder-chairman who had built the group's semiconductor dominance through the legendary "New Management" declaration at Frankfurt in 1993 — the speech in which he told executives to "change everything except your wife and children" — would remain hospitalised until his death on 25 October 2020. For the intervening six years, Lee Jae-yong, then Vice Chairman and the third-generation heir, ran the conglomerate without the formal title his father had carried since 1987.

The period was not without turbulence. In 2017, Lee Jae-yong was arrested in connection with the broader Choi Soon-sil corruption scandal that brought down President Park Geun-hye's government. He was convicted of bribery and embezzlement, served portions of his sentence, and was released on parole in August 2021. A presidential pardon followed in August 2022. Two months later, in October 2022, Samsung Electronics' board formalised what markets had long treated as settled: Lee Jae-yong was appointed Executive Chairman, assuming the title his father had held for more than three decades. The legal saga that had shadowed his ascent was, in the institutional framing preferred by Samsung's investor-relations office, now closed.

## Memory's Supercycle and Its Violent Reversal

Samsung's revenue trajectory through the post-Kun-hee transition illustrated the dominant role of memory in the group's economics. Revenue reached KRW 279.6 trillion (approximately USD 214 billion) in 2021, then climbed further to KRW 302.2 trillion (~USD 232 billion) in 2022 — a record at the time — carried by a pandemic-era surge in DRAM and NAND pricing that benefited every supplier in the commodity chain. [Samsung IR](https://www.samsung.com/global/ir/)

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (KRW trillions) | YoY Change |
|---|---|---|
| 2020 | 236.8 | — |
| 2021 | 279.6 | +18.1% |
| 2022 | 302.2 | +8.1% |
| 2023 | 258.9 | −14.3% |
| 2024 | 300.9 | +16.2% |

The reversal arrived with little ambiguity. Memory prices, which had begun softening in the second half of 2022 as PC and smartphone demand collapsed post-pandemic, fell precipitously through 2023. DRAM contract prices dropped more than fifty per cent from their 2022 peaks; NAND pricing fell further still. Samsung's Device Solutions division — the semiconductor unit encompassing DRAM, NAND, and HBM production alongside the foundry business — swung from being the group's principal profit engine to recording a full-year operating loss of approximately KRW 14.88 trillion (~USD 11.1 billion) for 2023. [Korea DART filing, 005930.KS, FY2023 annual report] The group's consolidated operating profit for the year collapsed to approximately KRW 6.57 trillion (~USD 4.9 billion), down from KRW 43.4 trillion (~USD 32.5 billion) in 2022 — a contraction that rivalled the worst memory downturns of the preceding two decades.

The quarterly cadence of 2023 was a study in sequential deterioration followed by tentative stabilisation. First-quarter operating profit across the group registered approximately KRW 640 billion (~USD 475 million), compared with KRW 14.1 trillion in the equivalent period of 2022. The Device Solutions division alone contributed operating losses in each of the first three quarters. By the fourth quarter, a modest price recovery in DRAM and an early improvement in NAND inventories began to stabilise the figures, though the full-year damage was already recorded.

Lee Jae-yong's public commentary during the trough period was characteristically restrained in the Korean chaebol fashion — broad strategic language in place of specific forward guidance. In earnings call communications, management acknowledged the inventory correction across the memory supply chain and signalled continued capital expenditure discipline, framing the downturn as a cyclical phenomenon the company had navigated before. The message to shareholders was one of institutional patience rather than structural alarm.

## The HBM3E Qualification Problem

What distinguished the 2023-2025 cycle from prior memory downturns was the emergence of a structural competitive dimension that a simple pricing recovery could not resolve. High-bandwidth memory — the stacked DRAM architecture critical to AI accelerator performance — had transformed from a niche product category into the highest-margin, highest-stakes segment of the memory industry. SK Hynix, Samsung's principal Korean rival, had invested aggressively in HBM capacity and customer relationships; by the time NVIDIA's H100 GPU reached volume production in 2023, SK Hynix held the dominant supply position for HBM3. [Bloomberg, Reuters]

Samsung's HBM3E qualification challenge at NVIDIA became the defining strategic narrative of the Lee Jae-yong era's early chapter. HBM3E — the generation following HBM3, offering higher bandwidth and capacity per stack — began volume production at SK Hynix in early 2024, with the Incheon-based rival announcing mass shipments in March of that year. Samsung, despite possessing comparable technical specifications on paper, encountered difficulties with yield and thermal performance sufficient to delay its own qualification. Reports through 2024 consistently placed Samsung in a secondary position relative to SK Hynix in the queue for NVIDIA HBM3E orders, with Micron Technology — the sole American DRAM producer — also securing qualification on an accelerated timeline. [DigiTimes; TrendForce]

The commercial consequences were direct. NVIDIA's AI accelerator roadmap — encompassing the H100, H200, and subsequently the Blackwell-architecture B200 — absorbed HBM3E at volumes that made qualification a prerequisite for meaningful revenue participation in the AI infrastructure cycle. SK Hynix's early lock on the supply relationship translated into margin premium and volume certainty that Samsung, entering the cycle from a qualification lag, could not immediately replicate.

Kye-Hyun Kyung, Vice Chairman and CEO of the Device Solutions division, addressed the HBM position in investor communications through 2024, characterising the qualification process as a technical challenge being resolved through engineering engagement with key customers. Samsung's position, per its official communications, was that it remained committed to the HBM3E qualification process and to the broader HBM4 generation transition that would follow — an implicit acknowledgement that the window for HBM3E primacy was narrowing even as recovery efforts continued.

## 2024 Recovery and the Incomplete Redemption

Samsung Electronics' 2024 revenue reached KRW 300.9 trillion (~USD 226 billion), recovering to within a fraction of the 2022 record. [Samsung IR] Memory pricing recovered across both DRAM and NAND as the inventory correction exhausted itself and AI-driven server demand absorbed production. The Device Solutions division returned to operating profitability, reversing the prior year's losses across multiple consecutive quarters and allowing the group's consolidated operating profit to rebuild toward the scale of prior cyclical peaks.

The recovery narrative carried an asterisk. The HBM3E qualification lag meant that Samsung captured a smaller share of the highest-value tier of the memory recovery than its installed production capacity would otherwise have implied. The AI-infrastructure spending cycle that drove server DRAM demand also concentrated disproportionate value in HBM — precisely the segment where Samsung's qualification position remained contested. The company continued to report progress in customer qualification engagements, and by the latter part of 2024 reports indicated Samsung had secured some HBM3E qualification in limited scope, though the structural gap relative to SK Hynix in the NVIDIA supply chain persisted through the frozen snapshot window. [Reuters; TrendForce]

On the foundry side — the contract manufacturing business operated under Samsung Foundry and led by President Kim Yong-kwan — the competitive position against TSMC remained the other long-run structural challenge of the Lee Jae-yong era. Samsung had introduced its 3-nanometre GAA (Gate-All-Around) transistor architecture in June 2022, nominally ahead of TSMC's equivalent transition, but customer adoption of Samsung Foundry's advanced nodes lagged the Hsinchu-based leader's equivalent generations. TSMC retained the most advanced fabless customers — Apple, NVIDIA, AMD — at the leading edge, with Samsung Foundry's customer roster concentrated in second-tier design houses and internal Samsung system LSI products. [FT; DigiTimes]

## The Lee Era's Strategic Mandate

The formal consolidation of Lee Jae-yong's authority as Executive Chairman in October 2022 — coinciding almost precisely with the onset of the memory downturn — placed the third-generation heir at the helm of a company navigating its most challenging earnings environment in a decade, simultaneously confronting structural competitive displacement in the highest-growth segment of its core business.

The leadership structure assembled around Lee Jae-yong through this period reflected the dual-track operational architecture Samsung had maintained across the Device Solutions and Device eXperience divisions. Han Jong-hee retained responsibility for the mobile and consumer electronics portfolio — including the Galaxy smartphone franchise, which held global unit leadership ahead of Apple through the period, and the Visual Display business that had led global television market share for approximately two decades. CFO Park Hark-kyu managed the capital allocation and investor communication function through the trough and partial recovery cycle.

The generational succession that Lee Kun-hee had begun engineering in the late 1980s had arrived at its institutional completion. Whether the era it inaugurated would be defined by the HBM3E recovery or by the longer-cycle ambitions of HBM4 and advanced foundry competition remained, at the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026, an open question — one whose answer would hinge as much on NVIDIA's qualification decisions as on the engineering choices made in Samsung's Hwaseong fabrication complex.

chapters.title: Lee Jae-yong, division leadership, and the Korean chaebol board
chapters.body:
## The Succession Arc

The formal investiture of Lee Jae-yong as Executive Chairman of Samsung Electronics in October 2022 closed a succession arc that had stretched, through courtrooms and hospital corridors, across nearly a decade. When his father Lee Kun-hee suffered a myocardial infarction in May 2014 and never returned to active management, the third-generation heir assumed de facto control of the world's largest memory-chip and consumer-electronics conglomerate with no title commensurate with his authority. He held the Vice Chairman designation until his father's death on 25 October 2020 rendered the question of formal succession unavoidable. A further two years of legal proceedings intervened before the path finally cleared.

The lineage began with founder Lee Byung-chul, who established Samsung as a dried-fish and noodle trading company in 1938 in Suwon and pivoted the group into electronics manufacturing with the founding of Samsung Electronics in January 1969. Lee Kun-hee, his third son, assumed the chairmanship in 1987 following his father's death and executed what historians of Korean industry still consider one of the most disciplined industrial-policy bets of the twentieth century: the decision to compete in memory semiconductors against Micron Technology and Japan's Toshiba and NEC at a moment when Korean manufacturing wages afforded only a slender cost advantage. By the early 1990s Samsung had become the world's largest DRAM producer. Under Lee Kun-hee's thirty-three-year tenure the group's revenues grew from roughly KRW 10 trillion to more than KRW 260 trillion (approximately USD 200 billion at mid-2020 exchange rates), and the Samsung Electronics common share became one of the most widely held equities in Asia.

Lee Jae-yong, born in January 1968, read East Asian History at Seoul National University, completed an MBA at Keio University in Tokyo, and enrolled in the doctoral programme at Harvard Business School, which he left without a degree. He joined Samsung Electronics full-time in 1991 and held a succession of operational roles across the company's global sales and strategy functions before being named to the board in 2010 and elevated to Vice Chairman in 2012. The incapacitation of his father two years later deposited on him the daily burden of chairing the group's council meetings and representing its semiconductor interests to customers, suppliers, and heads of state, while his formal rank remained a tier below the position he was effectively exercising.

## Legal Proceedings and the Path to Formal Chairmanship

The interval between de facto succession and formal title was not purely administrative. Lee Jae-yong became the central figure in two separate criminal proceedings that shaped both the governance narrative around Samsung and the broader Korean public debate about chaebol accountability.

The first case arose from the administration of President Park Geun-hye. Prosecutors alleged that Samsung had channelled approximately KRW 43 billion (around USD 35 million at prevailing rates) to foundations controlled by Park's confidante Choi Soon-sil in exchange for government support for a 2015 merger of Samsung C&T and Cheil Industries — a transaction that consolidated Lee Jae-yong's ownership stake in the group structure. Lee was convicted in a 2017 trial, released on appeal in 2018, and ultimately retried; in January 2021 the Seoul High Court handed down a sentence of two years and six months. He was imprisoned until August 2021, when he received a parole release on humanitarian grounds.

In August 2022, President Yoon Suk-yeol granted a special pardon restoring Lee Jae-yong's civil rights — a decision the Yoon administration justified on national-economic grounds, citing the chip-investment decisions that Samsung would need to make in competition with TSMC and US-subsidised facilities. Two months later, in October 2022, the Samsung Electronics board formally appointed him Executive Chairman, the title that had been structurally vacant since Lee Kun-hee's death and functionally vacant since his 2014 incapacitation. The appointment formalised what markets had long priced in: that Lee Jae-yong was, and had been for years, the principal decision-maker at the group.

## Device Solutions: Kye-Hyun Kyung

The operational executive machinery beneath the Executive Chairman divides Samsung Electronics into its two principal divisions. Device Solutions — the semiconductor arm encompassing Memory, Foundry, and System LSI — is led by [Kye-Hyun Kyung](https://www.samsung.com/global/ir/governance/management/), who held the title of Vice Chairman and co-CEO alongside Han Jong-hee following the leadership reshuffle that Samsung executed in late 2022 and formalised through its March 2023 annual general meeting.

Kyung, a career semiconductor executive who rose through the DRAM engineering and operations chain, inherited a division at an inflection point. The Memory business had run at cyclically elevated margins through 2021 and into early 2022 on pandemic-era demand, then collided with one of the sector's sharpest inventory corrections as hyperscaler capital expenditure paused and PC demand collapsed. At the same time, the Foundry business was navigating the transition from 7nm and 5nm process nodes to its 3nm gate-all-around architecture — the technology Samsung introduced to commercial production in 2022, ahead of TSMC's own GAA transition — while struggling to sustain yield rates capable of satisfying advanced logic customers.

The most consequential challenge inside Device Solutions, however, was not the cycle or the nodes but the HBM product line. SK Hynix had delivered production-ready HBM3 to NVIDIA in volume ahead of Samsung and had extended that lead into HBM3E, the 36-gigabyte stacks that NVIDIA specified for its H200 and subsequent accelerator platforms. Samsung's HBM3E qualification at NVIDIA became a running strategic embarrassment: the company that had invented DRAM and held the number-one position in the broader market was running behind its domestic rival in the product category that carried the highest average selling price and the most direct exposure to the AI infrastructure build-out. Kyung publicly acknowledged the qualification challenge in Samsung's investor communications, framing the HBM4 development programme as the vehicle through which Samsung would close and then reverse the gap.

## Device eXperience: Han Jong-hee

Han Jong-hee holds the parallel co-CEO designation for Device eXperience, the division containing Mobile Experience, Visual Display, and Digital Appliances. Han had served as head of Visual Display — Samsung's television business — before his elevation to the DX divisional leadership, and his trajectory reflected the continued strategic importance Samsung attached to its premium consumer brand even as semiconductor revenue commanded more of the group's investor narrative.

Mobile Experience, led at the product level by TM Roh (Roh Tae-moon) as President of the MX division, remained the single largest revenue contributor within DX. The Galaxy S series anchored Samsung's high-ASP smartphone positioning; the Galaxy Z Fold and Z Flip foldable lines, which Roh had championed through their iterative hardware and hinge engineering improvements, offered a product-category differentiation unavailable from Apple. Galaxy AI — the on-device and cloud-integrated generative features Samsung introduced across the Galaxy S24 series in early 2024 and expanded into subsequent hardware generations — represented the software dimension of MX's competitive response to the integration advantages Apple enjoyed through its silicon and operating-system co-design.

Within Foundry, Kim Yong-kwan served as President of Samsung Foundry and carried the direct responsibility for closing the yield and customer-confidence gap against TSMC. Samsung Foundry had secured Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Gen 1 as a flagship customer for its 4nm node, but a widely reported yield problem resulted in Qualcomm shifting significant volume of subsequent generations to TSMC. The recovery of credibility with advanced logic customers — NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, and the hyperscaler custom-silicon programmes — defined the central operational mandate of the Foundry business through this period.

## Harman and the Automotive Vector

Samsung's acquisition of Harman International in 2017 for approximately USD 8 billion — the largest overseas acquisition in South Korean corporate history at the time — added a fourth organisational dimension to the group. Harman, headquartered in Stamford, Connecticut, owned the JBL, Harman Kardon, AKG, and Mark Levinson audio brands alongside a substantial connected-car electronics business supplying infotainment systems to BMW, Toyota, and other global OEMs. James Park served as Harman's Chief Executive Officer, managing a business whose strategic rationale had shifted over the years from consumer audio premium-brand leverage toward its automotive electronics positioning at a moment when vehicle software content was rapidly expanding.

## Board Composition and Chaebol Governance

Samsung Electronics' board as constituted through the frozen snapshot of May 2026 comprised four inside directors — Lee Jae-yong, Kyung, Han, and CFO Park Hark-kyu — alongside six independent directors, a composition calibrated to Korean Stock Exchange listing requirements that mandate independent director majorities at large-cap issuers.

| Director | Role | Category |
|---|---|---|
| Lee Jae-yong | Executive Chairman | Executive |
| Kye-Hyun Kyung | Vice Chairman, Device Solutions CEO | Executive |
| Han Jong-hee | Vice Chairman, Device eXperience CEO | Executive |
| Park Hark-kyu | President, CFO | Executive |
| Lee Hee-tae | Lead Independent Director | Independent |
| Kim Sun-uk | Independent Director | Independent |
| Heo Eun-nyeong | Independent Director | Independent |
| Cho Hye-kyung | Independent Director | Independent |
| Yoo Myung-hee | Independent Director | Independent |
| Kim Han-jo | Independent Director | Independent |

*Source: [Samsung Electronics IR — Board of Directors](https://www.samsung.com/global/ir/governance/board-of-directors/)*

Lee Hee-tae served as Lead Independent Director, a role with particular structural significance at a company where a single executive family exercised controlling influence through a layered cross-shareholding structure rather than a direct majority ownership stake. The Korean chaebol model — in Samsung's case, a web of inter-group holdings running through Samsung Life Insurance, Samsung C&T, and other affiliates — means that governance accountability flows through the independent director tier and the minority shareholder protection mechanisms of Korean corporate law rather than through conventional owner-controller alignment.

Yoo Myung-hee, the former Minister of Trade, Industry and Energy and Korea's chief negotiator in the US-Korea Free Trade Agreement renegotiation, brought a trade-and-policy dimension to the board whose relevance had become more acute as the CHIPS Act and analogous industrial-policy instruments in Japan and Europe restructured the geography of semiconductor investment. Her appointment signalled the degree to which Samsung's board had been constituted to provide policy intelligence alongside conventional fiduciary oversight.

The governance architecture remained the subject of scrutiny from international institutional investors. Elliott Management's campaigns against the 2015 C&T–Cheil merger and the 2017 Samsung Group restructuring proposals had left a residue of activist vigilance among global fund managers holding the GDR and common share. The reforms extracted in subsequent proxy seasons — audit-committee independence, executive compensation disclosure, and the progressive strengthening of the Lead Independent Director role — represented incremental movement toward the governance norms expected by MSCI and FTSE index weighting methodologies, without fundamentally displacing the Lee family's structural control.
