Park Hark-kyu as CFO bridged the executive and governance dimensions of this architecture. His responsibilities across financial planning, treasury, and investor relations positioned him as the interlocutor between Lee Jae-yong's strategic direction, the operational leadership of Kyung and Han, and the capital markets that were, through the HBM and foundry cycles, rendering a verdict on whether Samsung's multi-decade engineering and manufacturing supremacy could survive the most compressed period of competitive realignment the semiconductor industry had experienced since the Japanese memory exodus of the 1980s.

chapters.title: NVIDIA, hyperscalers, smartphone customers, Foundry customers, global manufacturing
chapters.body:
## The NVIDIA Account: Chasing SK Hynix's Lead

No customer defined Samsung's memory division ambitions in the HBM era more sharply than NVIDIA. As the California chip designer's data-centre GPU revenue surged from roughly $2.7 billion in fiscal year 2022 to more than $90 billion by fiscal 2025, the allocation of high-bandwidth memory on each successive GPU generation — H100, H200, Blackwell — became one of the most consequential procurement decisions in the semiconductor industry. Samsung arrived late to that table, and the gap proved difficult to close.

SK Hynix had cemented its position as NVIDIA's principal HBM supplier through the Hopper generation, shipping HBM3 in volume from late 2022 while Samsung and Micron trailed in qualifications. When NVIDIA moved to the H200 — requiring HBM3E in 12-high stack configuration — SK Hynix again shipped first, with qualification confirmed in late 2023 and mass supply underway well before Samsung could match it. The consequence was visible in market-share data compiled by [TrendForce](https://trendforce.com): SK Hynix held roughly 50 percent of global HBM revenue through 2024, with Samsung in the 40-percent range on a mix of older-generation product, and Micron taking an emerging single-digit share on HBM3E entry volume.

Samsung's HBM3E qualification struggle at NVIDIA centred on thermal management and yield. The 12-high stack configuration generates substantial heat under sustained inference workloads; sources familiar with NVIDIA's qualification process, as reported by [Bloomberg](https://bloomberg.com) and the [Korea Economic Daily](https://www.kedglobal.com), indicated Samsung's samples exhibited thermal performance below the threshold required for GB200 NVL72 rack-scale systems. Samsung management, on the fourth-quarter 2024 earnings call, acknowledged the gap while pointing to the HBM4 generation as the expected inflection point — arguing that Samsung's DRAM process technology would prove a differentiating factor on the logic-base-die architecture that HBM4 requires. The pivot to HBM4 represented a bet that Samsung could reassert leadership at the next node transition rather than contesting each incremental HBM3E configuration. Qualification work at NVIDIA was continuing as of the frozen snapshot date.

## Hyperscalers: The Infrastructure Dividend

Beyond NVIDIA, Samsung's memory and storage divisions held broad exposure to hyperscaler capital expenditure. Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Meta collectively spent more than $200 billion on infrastructure in calendar 2024, with DRAM and NAND occupying a growing share of server bill-of-materials as AI inference workloads expanded from training clusters to production deployments.

Samsung's enterprise SSD line — the PM9A3, PM9C1a, and successor NVMe families — occupied prominent positions in hyperscaler procurement, benefiting from the DDR5 transition cycle that required new server platform deployments across the major cloud fleets. Samsung's DDR5 server DRAM qualified at hyperscaler memory labs and shipped in volume through 2024 as the industry completed the DDR4-to-DDR5 migration. Samsung IR materials cited data-centre DRAM and enterprise storage as the primary drivers of the KRW 300.9 trillion (~$226 billion) revenue recovery in 2024 off the 2023 trough.

The structural dynamics favoured Samsung's scale. With wafer capacity at its Pyeongtaek complex — the largest semiconductor manufacturing site by floor area in the world — Samsung could offer supply security that smaller competitors could not match. Hyperscalers building sovereign AI infrastructure increasingly valued dual-sourcing disciplines, providing Samsung a stable procurement floor even in cycles when SK Hynix held the performance edge on HBM.

## Smartphone Ecosystem: Galaxy and the Component Web

Samsung's DX division shipped an estimated 224 million smartphones in 2024, according to [IDC](https://idc.com), retaining the global unit-volume leadership it had held for more than a decade. The Galaxy S24 series — particularly the S24 Ultra, marketed around on-device "Galaxy AI" features — was positioned as Samsung's response to Apple's intelligence-era product cycle.

Yet the smartphone customer relationship extended well beyond Samsung's own Galaxy portfolio. Samsung Display — a subsidiary — supplied OLED panels to Apple for iPhone models, a relationship generating tens of trillions of won annually that persisted despite fierce brand competition at the handset level. Samsung's memory division supplied LPDDR5X DRAM and UFS 4.0 storage to Android OEMs including Xiaomi, OPPO, and vivo across the broader ecosystem. The component revenue gave Samsung's DS division a floor partially insulated from the cyclical fortunes of the Galaxy brand itself: when Chinese OEM market share expanded across Southeast Asia and emerging markets, Samsung's memory revenue frequently followed.

The Harman subsidiary — acquired in 2017 for approximately $8 billion — added an automotive and premium audio customer channel that sat outside the traditional semiconductor and handset relationships. JBL, Harman Kardon, and AKG brand products reached automotive OEM customers globally, a business less correlated with the memory cycle that anchored DS division earnings.

## Foundry: A Narrowing but Committed Customer Base

Samsung Foundry entered the 3nm generation as the first in the industry to deploy gate-all-around transistor architecture, completing the first commercial 3GAA tapeouts in mid-2022 ahead of TSMC's N3 risk production. The technical first-mover position did not immediately translate into customer breadth.

Qualcomm, historically one of Samsung Foundry's anchor customers for mobile application processor production, shifted the Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 and subsequently the 8 Gen 3 substantially to TSMC N4 and N3 processes, with yield reliability widely cited as the determining factor. The migration was significant: Qualcomm's Snapdragon line represents some of the largest mobile AP volume globally, and its move to TSMC narrowed Samsung Foundry's advanced-node revenue base in precisely the period when the foundry was attempting to establish its 4nm and 3nm credentials.

Google remained a Samsung Foundry customer through the Tensor G-series programme. IBM's Power10 processor line ran on Samsung processes. The foundry also maintained customers in automotive and power management segments less prominent in industry coverage. Samsung Foundry's stated ambition — articulated across investor materials and the Samsung Foundry Forum event series — was to capture share in AI accelerator logic silicon beyond its own System LSI products. NVIDIA's Hopper and Blackwell GPU dies ran exclusively at TSMC, but Samsung pursued conversations around future allocation as total AI accelerator volume expanded well beyond any single supplier's comfortable capacity. The 2nm SF2 process was in development through the period covered here, with yield ramping toward commercial readiness; whether Samsung could offer TSMC-competitive yield at 2nm would be determinative for its ability to re-attract tier-one fabless customers.

## Global Manufacturing: Scale and Strategic Diversification

| Facility | Location | Primary Output |
|---|---|---|
| Pyeongtaek P1/P2/P3 | Gyeonggi-do, Korea | DRAM, NAND, HBM |
| Hwaseong | Gyeonggi-do, Korea | DRAM, Foundry (mature nodes) |
| Giheung | Gyeonggi-do, Korea | Legacy DRAM, R&D |
| Xi'an Phase 1/2 | Shaanxi, China | NAND Flash |
| Suzhou | Jiangsu, China | Memory packaging and modules |
| Austin S1/S2 | Texas, USA | Mature-node foundry |
| Taylor | Texas, USA | Advanced foundry (under construction) |
| Bac Ninh / Thai Nguyen | Vietnam | Galaxy smartphone assembly |
| Noida | India | Galaxy assembly |
| Tijuana | Mexico | Consumer electronics assembly |

Samsung's domestic Korean footprint remained the centre of gravity for advanced semiconductor production. Pyeongtaek — built out across three platform generations at cumulative capital investment measured in tens of trillions of won — concentrated leading-edge DRAM, NAND, and HBM capacity within a single complex. The scale provided process cost advantages that competitors struggled to replicate but embedded geographic concentration risk that regulators, customers, and Samsung's own strategic planners cited as motivation for international diversification.

Vietnam emerged as the anchor of Samsung's mobile manufacturing diversification strategy. With cumulative foreign direct investment exceeding $22 billion across facilities in Bac Ninh and Thai Nguyen provinces, Samsung employed approximately 100,000 workers in Vietnam and assembled a majority of its global Galaxy smartphone volume there. The progressive shift away from Chinese assembly, executed through the 2010s, reduced labour-cost exposure and pre-empted much of the trade-friction impact that intensified from 2018 onward.

In the United States, Samsung operated mature-node foundry fabs in Austin through its S1 and S2 facilities producing logic at 14nm and above. The strategic pivot toward advanced-node US production took shape through a KRW 20-plus trillion ($17 billion) investment announcement in Taylor, Texas — adjacent to Austin — for a new leading-edge foundry complex. Samsung received a preliminary agreement for approximately $6.4 billion in CHIPS Act grants from the US Department of Commerce, subject to domestic workforce and supply-chain conditions. Construction at Taylor proceeded through 2024 and into 2025, though production timelines slipped relative to initial announcements amid broader foundry demand recalibration.

## Geopolitical Exposure: The Xi'an Variable

Samsung's China exposure concentrated in the Xi'an NAND complex, housing Phase 1 and Phase 2 of its Chinese NAND production. [TrendForce](https://trendforce.com) industry estimates placed the facility at roughly 40 percent of Samsung's total NAND bit output at periods of peak utilisation — a fraction sufficiently large that any disruption would materially affect global supply and Samsung's own cost structure.

US export controls on advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment, tightened in October 2022 and again in October 2023, created a structural constraint on Samsung's ability to upgrade the Xi'an facility. Samsung obtained a "verified end-user" designation from the US Commerce Department — effectively a renewable waiver allowing US-origin equipment suppliers to continue servicing and supplying the Chinese facilities. The arrangement required periodic renewal and carried inherent political risk: any change in Commerce Department posture could freeze Samsung's ability to modernise Xi'an equipment, gradually rendering the facility less competitive as process technology advanced at its Korean and American peers.

The broader US-China exposure ran through the customer base as well. Chinese smartphone OEMs — Xiaomi, OPPO, vivo — represented meaningful DRAM and NAND procurement, while Huawei's restricted access to advanced US-origin technology had already restructured some supply pathways. Samsung navigated the regulatory landscape cautiously, maintaining customer relationships while adhering to US export control frameworks that continued to evolve with each successive Commerce Department rulemaking through the period covered here.

chapters.title: Where Samsung sits against SK Hynix, TSMC, Apple, broader competitive set
chapters.body:
## The Memory Battlefield: SK Hynix and the HBM Reckoning

For most of Samsung's modern history, its position atop the global DRAM market was the bedrock upon which everything else rested. In 2023 and into 2024, that bedrock shifted. The specific mechanism was the HBM — high-bandwidth memory — stack architecture that Nvidia's AI accelerator roadmap had made essential, and in which Samsung found itself occupying an uncomfortable third position behind the company it had spent decades defining itself against.

SK Hynix's dominance of HBM3 and HBM3E supply to Nvidia had its origins in a strategic bet the Icheon-based rival placed on AI training workloads several years before the market validated it. By the time Nvidia's H100 and H200 accelerators were shipping in volume through 2023 and 2024, SK Hynix was supplying the overwhelming majority of the HBM3E modules embedded in them. [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/) reported SK Hynix held roughly half of global HBM market revenue in 2024, with its position in the highest-margin HBM3E segment even more concentrated than its overall share implied.

Samsung's qualification struggle at Nvidia was not merely a yield problem, though yields were a significant component. The HBM stack assembly process — bonding multiple DRAM dies with through-silicon vias and attaching them directly to a logic die — demands thermal management and electrical performance specifications that Samsung's 8-high and 12-high HBM3E products found difficult to satisfy under Nvidia's validation protocols. Samsung's DS Division leadership acknowledged the delay on the company's first-quarter 2025 earnings call, indicating that HBM3E qualification remained in progress while the company redirected development attention toward HBM4.

| Metric | Samsung | SK Hynix | Micron |
|---|---|---|---|
| DRAM Market Share (2024E) | ~42% | ~33% | ~23% |
| HBM Revenue Share (2024E) | ~25% | ~53% | ~22% |
| HBM3E Nvidia Qualification | Delayed into 2025 | Qualified; primary supplier | Qualified late 2024 |
| HBM4 Volume Target | 2026 | 2026 | 2026 |

*Sources: [TrendForce](https://www.trendforce.com/); company filings; [DigiTimes](https://www.digitimes.com/)*

The table above reflects an uncomfortable reality for a company that invented many of the production processes underlying DRAM economics. Samsung remained the world's largest DRAM producer by overall revenue and volume share, but in the specific product segment commanding the highest per-gigabyte premium in the semiconductor industry's history, it was playing catch-up to a rival it once dwarfed.

## Micron's Emergence as a Third Competitor

Micron Technology's qualification of HBM3E at Nvidia in late 2024 added a second front to Samsung's competitive pressure in high-bandwidth memory. The Boise-based producer had historically been a distant third in DRAM market share and had no meaningful HBM presence before 2023. Its successful entry into Nvidia's supply chain demonstrated that the barriers to HBM qualification were surmountable and that Samsung's delay was company-specific rather than a product of structural complexity alone.

Micron's HBM3E specification — rated at 1.2 terabytes per second per stack — matched SK Hynix's product on headline throughput. Its cost structure further benefited from U.S. CHIPS Act capital subsidies flowing to its Boise and Manassas fabs, partially offsetting the yield learning-curve costs that new HBM entrants typically absorb. For Samsung, Micron's entry meant the window in which catching up to SK Hynix would restore any semblance of HBM duopoly pricing power was already closing. A three-supplier HBM market implies meaningfully different margin dynamics than the two-supplier construct Samsung might have targeted had it qualified on schedule.

## Foundry: The TSMC Chasm

In contract semiconductor manufacturing, the gap between Samsung Foundry and TSMC widened during the period under review in ways that did not track the companies' stated node comparisons. Samsung Foundry introduced its 3-nanometer gate-all-around process in June 2022 — technically ahead of TSMC's N3 node — and used the milestone to assert process technology leadership. In practice, customer adoption told a different story.

TSMC's N3 and N3E nodes attracted Apple's A17 Pro and M3 application processors, Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Gen 3, and AMD's Zen 5 compute chiplets, among other high-volume designs. Samsung Foundry's 3nm GAA found its primary customer in Samsung's own System LSI division — the Exynos 2500 mobile processor — while third-party tape-outs remained sparse. The distinction between process leadership on paper and process leadership as defined by yield-at-volume, design rule maturity, and IP ecosystem depth favored TSMC substantially.

| Metric | TSMC | Samsung Foundry | Intel Foundry |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue Market Share (2024E) | ~62% | ~13% | ~2% |
| Leading-Edge Flagship Customers | Apple, Qualcomm, AMD, Nvidia | Samsung System LSI; limited 3P | Intel internal |
| 2nm Node Status | N2 volume ramp 2025 | 2nm GAA in development | 18A delayed |
| Advanced EUV Capacity | Industry-leading installed base | Meaningful but substantially less | Ramping |

*Sources: [TrendForce](https://www.trendforce.com/); [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/); company filings*

TSMC's revenue share advantage — roughly five times Samsung Foundry's revenue — reflected compounding advantages in design enablement, IP partner ecosystems, and the customer-facing confidence built from consistently delivering at yield. Every major fabless company that had moved a flagship design to Samsung Foundry's leading edge and subsequently experienced yield-related delays had the option of moving to TSMC, and a meaningful number exercised it. The resulting customer concentration risk — where Samsung Foundry's leading-edge utilization depended heavily on its own upstream divisions — was structurally distinct from TSMC's diversified fabless customer base spanning the entirety of the global semiconductor industry.

## Intel Foundry Services: An Asymmetric Wildcard

Intel Foundry Services entered Samsung's competitive landscape not as an immediate threat to existing share but as a potential demand absorber for customers who might otherwise have diversified toward Samsung Foundry in search of a TSMC alternative. Intel's 18A process, built on RibbonFET gate-all-around architecture and backside power delivery, attracted stated interest from Microsoft and exploratory engagement from Broadcom — though timelines slipped materially through 2024 and into 2025. Should Intel Foundry eventually achieve competitive yield at advanced nodes, the implication for Samsung Foundry is a more crowded market for the TSMC-alternative demand that Samsung had been positioned to capture almost by default.

## Mobile: Apple and the Premium Profit Gap

In smartphone hardware, Samsung and Apple inhabit what appears from the outside to be a duopoly in premium devices but is more accurately described as a two-tier market in which Apple captures a disproportionate share of global smartphone operating profit. Apple's iPhone commanded operating margins in the premium tier that Samsung's Galaxy S series, despite competitive specifications, could not replicate — a function of Apple's vertical software-hardware integration, iOS ecosystem lock-in, and brand positioning in aspirational consumer markets worldwide.

Samsung's Galaxy S25 series, launched in early 2025 with Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite processors rather than the company's own Exynos silicon, reflected an implicit concession that Samsung's internal chip design had not achieved the performance-per-watt parity needed to anchor the flagship user experience. The decision to source externally for its own branded smartphones — while simultaneously competing to manufacture chips for Qualcomm's rivals through Samsung Foundry — illustrated the organizational tensions embedded in the DS/DX structure.

> "We are committed to expanding our Galaxy AI features across the portfolio and ensuring that our hardware platform delivers the differentiated experience our customers expect."

Apple's replacement cycle dynamics added a further structural headwind. iPhone upgrade cycles had lengthened as consumers held devices for three to four years, but Apple's installed base of approximately one billion active iPhone users continued generating services revenue that widened its effective margin advantage over Samsung in the aggregate device ecosystem. In the markets where Samsung commanded share — South Korea, Southeast Asia, parts of Europe — iPhone penetration had edged upward through 2024, particularly among younger demographics for whom the iOS ecosystem represented a social signaling mechanism as much as a technology choice.

## Chinese OEMs and the Mid-Tier Erosion

Below the premium tier, Samsung's Galaxy A and M series faced intensifying pressure from Chinese smartphone manufacturers — principally Xiaomi, OPPO, vivo, and a resurgent Huawei — across the price segments representing the highest volume in global smartphone shipments. Chinese OEM penetration of Southeast Asian, South Asian, Latin American, and Middle Eastern markets, which had constituted Samsung's primary volume growth geography, accelerated through 2024, with Xiaomi in particular posting market share gains across India and several ASEAN markets at Samsung's direct expense.

Huawei's return to the Chinese premium tier with the Mate 60 Pro — featuring a Kirin 9000S processor manufactured by SMIC at an estimated 7-nanometer-equivalent process — carried strategic significance beyond its unit volumes. It demonstrated that Chinese domestic semiconductor production could support competitive high-end device design, reducing Huawei's dependency on Samsung or SK Hynix memory components and signalling the trajectory of Chinese self-sufficiency in the device ecosystem. For Samsung, Huawei's resurgence cut into both hardware revenue and the component demand that Chinese device sales would otherwise have generated through Samsung's Memory division.

Xiaomi, OPPO, and vivo collectively controlled a majority of the sub-$400 smartphone market across emerging markets by 2024. Their manufacturing cost structures — benefiting from deep Chinese domestic supply chains and direct relationships with Chinese panel and component vendors — allowed pricing that Samsung's DX Division found structurally difficult to match without margin sacrifice.

## LG Electronics: The Chaebol Peer Marker

LG Electronics provides a useful reference point for understanding Samsung's consumer electronics competitive positioning, albeit one that grew less directly relevant after LG exited the mobile handset business in 2021. In the large-format display market, LG and Samsung remain the dominant global brands, though with divergent technology bets: LG's WOLED panel technology versus Samsung's QD-OLED and Neo QLED lines compete for the premium living-room display segment, with LG Display supplying OLED panels not only to its parent company but to Sony — with whom Samsung competes directly.

The more structurally relevant LG comparison, however, is as a reminder of what a Korean chaebol's competitive position looks like when one of its core business lines is abandoned rather than defended. Samsung's decision to maintain its mobile business through a period of margin compression — rather than follow LG's 2021 exit — reflected Lee Jae-yong's read that the Galaxy ecosystem's role as a platform for Samsung components, services, and AI features made it worth defending even at diminished profitability in certain tiers.

## Synthesis: Pressure at the Highest-Margin Nodes

Taken together, Samsung's competitive landscape as of the first half of 2026 presented a company that retained structural scale advantages — the largest DRAM producer, the second-largest foundry, a top-three global smartphone brand — while facing targeted competitive erosion at precisely the highest-margin points of each of those markets. SK Hynix's lead in HBM3E, TSMC's dominance of advanced foundry customer acquisition, Apple's premium margin advantage in mobile, and Chinese OEMs' mid-tier pricing pressure constituted distinct challenges arising from different competitive dynamics but sharing a common thread: Samsung's advantage in scale and vertical integration was least effective where the industry's most attractive economics had migrated.

The HBM4 generation — targeting 2026 volume production across Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron — represented Samsung's clearest near-term opportunity to reset the competitive narrative in memory. Samsung Foundry's 2nm roadmap, if it achieved yield metrics closer to TSMC's N2 performance, could similarly reopen the third-party customer conversations that had stalled at 3nm. Neither outcome was assured. What the competitive map made clear was that Samsung's response across each of these fronts would determine whether the company's multi-division scale remained a source of integrated competitive strength — or became a structure too broad to defend any single frontier at the standard its own history had established.

chapters.title: From 1969 founding through Lee successions, memory cycles, HBM challenge
chapters.body:
## A Semiconductor Empire Built on a Rice-Trading Legacy

Samsung Electronics was incorporated on 13 January 1969 as a modest consumer electronics assembler in Suwon, South Korea, a spin-off from Lee Byung-chul's Samsung Group trading conglomerate that had itself begun life selling dried fish and noodles in 1938. The founding mandate was straightforward: manufacture black-and-white televisions for a domestic market newly flush with wages from the postwar industrialisation drive that Park Chung-hee's government was orchestrating across the peninsula. That the company would, within five decades, become the world's largest memory chip producer, operate the planet's second-largest contract semiconductor foundry, and ship more smartphones than any rival was not foreordained — it was the product of a series of audacious, often costly strategic bets made across three generations of the Lee family.

The critical inflection came in 1983, when Lee Byung-chul committed Samsung to DRAM production over the objections of advisers who argued the capital requirements and cycle volatility were ruinous for a latecomer. The "Tokyo Declaration," as Lee's pronouncement became known, committed Samsung to memory semiconductors at a time when Intel and Japanese rivals held every significant process advantage. The first 64K DRAM rolled off Samsung's Kiheung line within eighteen months, behind the frontier but within striking range — and the pattern of aggressive capital deployment that would define Samsung's competitive posture for the next four decades was established.

## Lee Kun-hee and the New Management Declaration

Lee Byung-chul died in November 1987, passing effective control to his third son, Lee Kun-hee, who was formally appointed Chairman of Samsung Electronics that same year. The transition coincided with a period of dangerous complacency: Samsung's consumer electronics had achieved scale but not premium perception, and its semiconductor operations were still operating largely on licensed foreign technology. Lee Kun-hee's response was the "New Management" declaration delivered at the Frankfurt Marriott in June 1993, a speech that has since acquired the status of corporate scripture in Korean business culture. In it, he instructed Samsung's global executives to "change everything except your wife and children" — a blunt injunction to discard the volume-and-cost logic of the chaebol model in favour of quality, design, and brand equity.

The declaration preceded the most sustained wealth-creation run in Korean corporate history. Through the 1990s, Samsung's DRAM operations captured global share as Japanese rivals retrenched under the Plaza Accord's aftermath. The 1997-98 Asian financial crisis devastated much of the chaebol sector, but Samsung Electronics emerged leaner and with expanded foundry capacity that would soon feed the coming mobile revolution. By the time the Galaxy S series launched in 2010 — directly contesting Apple's iPhone on features and price — Samsung had transitioned from a respected mid-tier manufacturer into a global first-tier brand. Lee Kun-hee's three-decade chairmanship saw revenue expand from a few trillion won to KRW 302.2 trillion (approximately USD 227 billion) at the 2022 peak.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (KRW trillions) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 2020 | 236.8 | Recovery from COVID-19 cycle disruption |
| 2021 | 279.6 | DRAM/NAND supercycle; memory ASP expansion |
| 2022 | 302.2 | Peak revenue; memory correction begins H2 |
| 2023 | 258.9 | Deep memory downturn trough |
| 2024 | 300.9 | Recovery; HBM ramp; ~USD 226B |

*Source: Samsung Electronics IR, [samsung.com/global/ir](https://www.samsung.com/global/ir/); Korea DART filings for 005930.KS*

Lee Kun-hee suffered a heart attack in May 2014 that left him incapacitated; he died in October 2020. His final years were spent largely outside active management, and yet the ownership architecture he had spent decades constructing — cross-shareholdings through Samsung Life Insurance, Samsung C&T, and Samsung Electronics itself — ensured that the family's grip on strategic decision-making was never in serious doubt.

## The Succession and the Legal Crucible

Lee Jae-yong, known internationally as Jay Y. Lee, had been accumulating operational authority since the mid-2000s and was appointed Vice Chairman of Samsung Electronics in 2012. His father's incapacitation in 2014 made the de facto transfer of control complete, though the formal title of Executive Chairman did not arrive until October 2022 — an eight-year interregnum shaped as much by Korean courts as by boardroom deliberation.

Lee Jae-yong's path to formal succession was interrupted by two criminal prosecutions arising from the 2015-16 chaebol-corruption scandal that also consumed President Park Geun-hye. The first trial ended in a suspended sentence; an appeals process and retrial resulted in a final 2.5-year prison term, a portion of which he served. His pardon in August 2022 by President Yoon Suk-yeol — framed explicitly in terms of national economic necessity at a moment of global semiconductor supply-chain stress — cleared the path for the October 2022 Executive Chairman appointment at Samsung Electronics' board meeting. [Korea JoongAng Daily](https://koreajoongangdaily.joins.com/) covered the appointment extensively as the formal completion of a succession that had been functionally underway for nearly a decade.

The leadership architecture that crystallised around Lee Jae-yong assigns operational management across two Vice Chairman and CEO roles: Kye-Hyun Kyung leads the Device Solutions division — encompassing memory, foundry, and System LSI — while Han Jong-hee leads the Device eXperience division covering Galaxy mobile, visual display, and digital appliances. Park Hark-kyu serves as President and CFO. Kim Yong-kwan heads Samsung Foundry as a distinct operating entity. The structure reflects the scale and complexity of a conglomerate that simultaneously competes in commodity DRAM, advanced packaging, contract semiconductor manufacturing, and mass-market consumer electronics within a single corporate envelope.

## The Memory Cycle and the HBM Reckoning

Samsung's revenue trajectory from 2022 to 2024 is a compressed study in semiconductor cyclicality. The 2022 revenue peak of KRW 302.2 trillion gave way to a KRW 258.9 trillion trough in 2023 as memory prices collapsed under inventory digestion across the PC, server, and smartphone supply chains. The magnitude of the correction — roughly KRW 43 trillion in lost revenue in a single fiscal year — was a reminder that Samsung's earnings remain structurally leveraged to DRAM and NAND pricing cycles in a way that no amount of consumer electronics diversification has fully neutralised.

The 2024 recovery to KRW 300.9 trillion (approximately USD 226 billion) was driven by memory price normalisation and the early stages of an AI-infrastructure-driven supercycle in high-bandwidth memory. It was here that Samsung confronted the most strategically uncomfortable development of the Lee Jae-yong era: SK Hynix's emergence as the decisive leader in HBM3 and HBM3E supply to NVIDIA.

HBM — high-bandwidth memory — is the stacked DRAM architecture that AI accelerators require in volume. NVIDIA's H100 and H200 systems, the principal hardware of the generative AI infrastructure build-out, consumed HBM3E at scale. SK Hynix, Samsung's smaller domestic rival, had invested earlier and more aggressively in the thermal and yield engineering challenges that HBM stacking demands, and secured NVIDIA qualification ahead of Samsung. Through 2024 and into 2025, Samsung's HBM3E product struggled to clear NVIDIA's qualification process, leaving SK Hynix — and in a secondary position Micron — to capture the majority of the most margin-accretive memory revenue available in the market. [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/) and [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/) reported repeatedly on Samsung's remediation efforts across this period, with the gap framed as both a technical and reputational challenge for the world's largest memory producer.

## Forward Catalysts: HBM4, Foundry, and the Galaxy S26 Cycle

The forward-looking case for Samsung rests on three catalysts that were, as of the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026, each at varying stages of resolution.

The first is HBM4 qualification at NVIDIA and the broader AI accelerator customer base. HBM4, the next-generation standard that advances bandwidth, capacity per stack, and thermal performance, represents Samsung's opportunity to leapfrog — or at least narrow — the gap that SK Hynix established in HBM3E. The Device Solutions division under Kye-Hyun Kyung has framed HBM4 readiness as a top-tier priority, with Samsung's vertical integration — owning both the DRAM manufacturing and advanced packaging operations under one roof — cited as a structural advantage in the aggressive yield ramp that HBM4 economics require.

The second catalyst is Samsung Foundry's advanced node roadmap. Samsung introduced the industry's first commercial 3nm gate-all-around transistor in 2022, beating TSMC to GAA by at least one process generation. The competitive prize is winning meaningful volume allocation from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, and the hyperscaler custom silicon programmes — customers who have overwhelmingly allocated their most advanced process nodes to TSMC through the 2nm transition window. Kim Yong-kwan's Samsung Foundry has positioned the 2nm node and its advanced packaging integration as the inflection point at which yield and price will make dual-sourcing economically rational for at least a portion of that customer base.

The third is the Galaxy S26 product cycle and the broader Galaxy AI narrative. TM Roh's Mobile Experience division has bet heavily on on-device AI features as a differentiator against both Apple and Chinese handset makers. The Galaxy S26 refresh — expected on the annual cadence — carries the dual mandate of sustaining Samsung's unit leadership in Android premium and demonstrating that Galaxy AI capabilities justify a narrower discount to iPhone pricing in the markets where margin extraction actually matters.

Each of these catalysts is real. Each carries execution risk commensurate with its strategic weight. The Lee family's three-generation record suggests that Samsung has navigated harder straits before — the 1983 DRAM bet, the 1997 crisis, the Galaxy launch into a market Apple appeared to own. Whether the HBM4 window closes the gap or extends it will be the most closely watched datapoint in global semiconductor coverage through the remainder of 2026.

chapters.title: Memory technology, Foundry advanced nodes, mobile/display IP, Bell-Labs-equivalent research
chapters.body:
## The Patent Machine

Samsung Electronics' position as one of the world's most prolific semiconductor patent filers was not accidental. The company ranked among the top recipients of US utility patents for multiple consecutive years through the early 2020s, a reflection of a research apparatus assembled across five decades of capital-intensive accumulation and a corporate culture — inherited from founder Lee Byung-chul and codified by Lee Kun-hee — that treated intellectual property as strategic deterrence as much as commercial asset. By the mid-2020s, that apparatus faced its most demanding test: SK Hynix had seized the initiative in high-bandwidth memory, TSMC was reinforcing its advanced-node moat, and Samsung's engineering leadership had to convert a portfolio built on incumbency into one capable of closing two simultaneous gaps.

## DRAM Scaling and the Angstrom Frontier

Samsung's dominance in DRAM rested on a lineage of process-node transitions that competitors tracked like a metronome. Through the late 2010s and early 2020s, Samsung advanced its DRAM through successive sub-ten-nanometre generations — designated internally by the company as 1x, 1y, 1z, 1a, 1b, and 1c nodes — compressing cell area while preserving refresh characteristics and signal integrity. The 1a node, introduced at volume in 2021, represented the leading edge of planar scaling; the 1b and 1c generations pushed cell heights further, requiring increasingly sophisticated extreme-ultraviolet lithography and novel capacitor dielectric materials to sustain the charge retention necessary for DDR5 and LPDDR5X specifications.

The deepest IP moat in DRAM lay in the capacitor stack — the high-k dielectric materials, titanium nitride electrode engineering, and aspect-ratio-etching techniques that allowed Samsung to stack sufficient charge storage into a shrinking cell footprint. These process patents, accumulated across decades at Hwaseong and Pyeongtaek, formed a formidable barrier that constrained how quickly Micron or SK Hynix could replicate each node transition without licensing exposure. Samsung's DRAM patent position was reinforced by its vertical integration: it designed its own deposition and etch equipment specifications in collaboration with Applied Materials, Tokyo Electron, and ASML, sometimes deriving IP through co-development agreements that gave it an early window on tooling capability.

## V-NAND and Three-Dimensional Flash

Samsung introduced vertical NAND — branded V-NAND — in 2013 with the 840 EVO consumer solid-state drive, becoming the first manufacturer to bring three-dimensional NAND to commercial volume. The architecture replaced the horizontal bit-cell layout of planar NAND with vertically stacked charge-trap cell strings, sidestepping the lithographic scaling limits that had begun to erode planar flash reliability below ~15nm. By the early 2020s, Samsung was stacking beyond 230 layers in a single pass — a technique it called single-stack; competitors Kioxia/Western Digital and Micron pursued bonded multi-stack approaches — and was developing string-stacking architectures to push further without proportional increases in deposition cycle time.

The competitive significance was twofold: layer count determined areal density and therefore cost per gigabyte, and the process IP embedded in high-aspect-ratio channel-hole etching, word-line fill, and cell-string integration represented barriers to fast imitation. Samsung's V-NAND layer roadmap ran ahead of its own consumer product launches; by the time a product shipped with a given layer count, the process engineers were typically two generations ahead in yield optimisation.

## HBM Packaging: The Ground Ceded and the Ground to Recover

High-bandwidth memory exposed the limits of process-IP leadership when system-integration and packaging execution diverged. HBM had originated as a joint development between AMD and SK Hynix, and SK Hynix leveraged its first-mover integration work to deliver HBM3 and HBM3E products ahead of Samsung's equivalent roadmap in 2023 and 2024. NVIDIA's preference for SK Hynix HBM3E in its H100 and H200 GPU platforms — driven by thermal performance, yield, and power-per-bandwidth metrics — was the strategic rebuke that defined Samsung's memory challenge heading into the latter half of the decade.

Samsung's HBM IP estate was substantive: it held broad patents on through-silicon via (TSV) formation, microbump interconnect arrays, and the non-conductive film underfill processes that mechanically coupled stacked DRAM dies to the base logic die. The technical difficulty lay not in the patent position but in manufacturing execution — achieving the TSV uniformity, die-stack planarity, and thermal interface quality that NVIDIA's qualification process demanded across high-volume production lots. Samsung's Device Solutions division characterised the HBM3E qualification effort as an ongoing engineering campaign; by the frozen snapshot date of May 2026, the company had publicly disclosed accelerated HBM4 development timelines, targeting a 12-high stack configuration with wider I/O interface counts that would, if successful, leapfrog the HBM3E generation rather than merely catching up to it.

## Foundry Advanced Nodes: GAA First, Yield Second

In June 2022, Samsung Foundry shipped the world's first commercial gate-all-around transistor node — the SF3E process, also described as 3nm GAA — beating TSMC's planned GAA introduction by roughly two years. The achievement was genuinely significant: replacing the FinFET gate geometry with a nanosheet transistor that wrapped the gate material around all four sides of the channel reduced leakage current and improved electrostatic control at geometries where FinFET architectures faced fundamental physical limits. Samsung's variant, which it branded Multi-Bridge Channel FET (MBCFET), used horizontally stacked silicon nanosheets of variable width — a tunable geometry that allowed designers to trade performance against power consumption by adjusting nanosheet dimensions.

[Samsung Foundry press releases, Samsung.com/global/ir](https://www.samsung.com/global/ir) noted that the SF3E node delivered a claimed 45 percent power reduction and 23 percent performance gain versus its 5nm predecessor. The technical IP underlying MBCFET — nanosheet formation, inner spacer engineering to isolate gate regions between sheets, and the source/drain epitaxy processes that determined carrier mobility — represented the core of Samsung Foundry's advanced-node patent portfolio. The problem, which Samsung publicly acknowledged through investor communications and which industry observers at [DigiTimes](https://www.digitimes.com) tracked through supply-chain signals, was that first-generation SF3E yields were insufficient to attract the large-volume AI accelerator customers — NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm — whose orders would have validated the foundry roadmap commercially.

The 2nm SF2 node, targeted for volume production in the 2025–2026 window, represented Samsung Foundry's attempt to advance the MBCFET architecture while simultaneously closing the yield gap with TSMC's N3 and N2 processes. The competitive landscape remained asymmetric: TSMC's installed advanced-node customer base generated learning-curve advantages in defect-density reduction that Samsung, with a thinner customer roster, replicated more slowly.

## Mobile and Display IP

Samsung's mobile IP portfolio was anchored by Exynos application processor development — the System LSI division's multi-year effort to build a competitive alternative to Qualcomm Snapdragon for Galaxy flagship devices — and by its ISOCELL imaging sensor line. ISOCELL, which Samsung commercialised from around 2013, embedded a physical isolation barrier between adjacent pixel photodiodes in the sensor array, reducing optical crosstalk and improving low-light performance; successive ISOCELL generations pushed pixel sizes below 0.6 micrometres while sustaining signal quality.

In display technology, Samsung Display — the subsidiary providing panels to the DX division — held fundamental IP in active-matrix organic LED and, increasingly, in foldable display hinge-glass integration. The Ultra-Thin Glass (UTG) used in the Galaxy Z Fold and Z Flip series, sourced through Schott and Corning partnerships but qualified and specified by Samsung engineering, involved proprietary cold-bending and surface-treatment IP that defined the minimum crease radius achievable without micro-fracture propagation. Samsung Display's under-panel camera technology, deployed in select Galaxy Z Fold iterations, embedded sub-pixel transparency patterns and compensation algorithms to reduce moiré artefacts — a system-level IP claim spanning display architecture and image processing simultaneously.

## Samsung Advanced Institute of Technology

At the apex of Samsung's research hierarchy sat the Samsung Advanced Institute of Technology (SAIT), established in 1987 in Suwon and functionally analogous — in corporate ambition if not academic culture — to Bell Laboratories in its mid-century role. SAIT operated with a remit to pursue research horizons beyond a five-year commercial horizon, staffing its programmes with PhDs recruited from KAIST, Seoul National University, MIT, and Stanford across disciplines from solid-state physics to materials chemistry to quantum information science.

SAIT's most commercially consequential output ran through the materials and process pipeline that eventually fed Samsung's manufacturing nodes: the high-k dielectric research that enabled sub-20nm DRAM capacitors, the hafnium-based ferroelectric work underlying FeRAM and next-generation non-volatile candidates, and early nanosheet transistor modelling that informed MBCFET design. Its longer-range programmes included silicon photonics integration research — relevant to future chiplet interconnect architectures — and neuromorphic computing hardware, areas where Samsung filed patents at a pace that signalled competitive intent without immediate commercialisation timelines.

The institute's structural importance was less about any single breakthrough than about sustaining the depth of materials and device physics knowledge across generation cycles. Samsung's history demonstrated that semiconductor leadership was lost and recovered at the process-node boundary — and SAIT's function was to ensure the company arrived at each boundary with the physical understanding necessary to clear it.

chapters.title: Memory cycle, HBM competition, Foundry-TSMC gap, geopolitical, chaebol governance
chapters.body:
## Memory Cycle Volatility

Samsung's financial architecture is built on a commodity that punishes the unlucky and rewards the patient. The memory division — spanning DRAM, NAND flash, and the emerging high-bandwidth memory category — has historically delivered the bulk of the company's operating profit during upswings and absorbed catastrophic losses in down cycles. The 2023 memory trough was among the deepest in a generation. [Group revenue fell from KRW 302.2 trillion (approximately USD 227 billion) in 2022 to KRW 258.9 trillion (USD 194 billion) in 2023](https://www.samsung.com/global/ir/financial-information/audited-financial-statements/) — a KRW 43.3 trillion contraction in a single fiscal year — as DRAM spot prices collapsed under the weight of inventory overhang accumulated during the pandemic-era demand surge.

The partial recovery to KRW 300.9 trillion in 2024 restored topline momentum but masked a structural shift in where the memory margin was being generated. Conventional DRAM remained a volume game, increasingly subject to price floors set by the three-oligopoly dynamics of Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron Technology. The more consequential question for Samsung's earnings trajectory through 2026 was whether it could claim a proportional share of the high-bandwidth memory market that had emerged as artificial-intelligence infrastructure's most inelastic demand segment.

Memory cycles have historically averaged four to five years peak to trough, and Samsung used downturns to press contrarian capital expenditure — maintaining fab investment when peers cut, emerging with process leadership when demand returned. That strategy succeeded in the early-2010s DRAM consolidation. Whether it proved as effective in an era where the premium tier of memory required a qualitatively different engineering capability was the first open question for investors.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (KRW T) | Revenue (USD B, approx.) |
|---|---|---|
| 2020 | 236.8 | 204 |
| 2021 | 279.6 | 242 |
| 2022 | 302.2 | 227 |
| 2023 | 258.9 | 194 |
| 2024 | 300.9 | 226 |

## The HBM4 Execution Test

No single competitive failure defined Samsung's 2024 more sharply than its inability to win primary qualification for HBM3E at NVIDIA. SK Hynix, which had invested early in the thermal and power architecture required by NVIDIA's H100 and H200 accelerators, held the principal supplier position throughout the year. [Samsung's HBM3E product encountered heat dissipation and yield challenges that delayed NVIDIA qualification](https://www.bloomberg.com/), costing Samsung meaningful allocation volume at precisely the moment AI infrastructure spending was accelerating most rapidly.

The stakes for HBM4 were correspondingly higher. HBM4 was expected to ship on NVIDIA's next generation of accelerators, and the performance requirements — bandwidth density, power envelope, thermal management — were meaningfully more demanding than HBM3E. Samsung's 12-layer HBM3E product was in late-stage qualification at multiple customers as of the frozen snapshot date, but the qualification gap with SK Hynix had not closed.

The execution risk was layered. First, Samsung had to close the yield gap with SK Hynix on current-generation product while simultaneously ramping HBM4 engineering. Second, NVIDIA's procurement process had become more concentrated — a qualification failure at one generation compounded into a structural disadvantage at the next as customer roadmap integration deepened. Third, [Micron Technology had entered the HBM3E qualification cycle at NVIDIA](https://www.reuters.com/), meaning Samsung faced a two-front competitive challenge: defending against Micron from below while attempting to recapture share from SK Hynix above.

Samsung leadership was measured in public statements about the timeline. The company declined to disclose specific HBM4 revenue targets, and investor communications framed the qualification trajectory in terms of multi-quarter process milestones rather than firm delivery dates — a posture that frustrated analysts seeking a more precise recovery schedule.

## Foundry's TSMC Gap

Samsung Foundry's introduction of its 3nm gate-all-around transistor process in 2022 was a genuine engineering milestone — the first commercial GAA node in production anywhere in the world. But it arrived ahead of the customer demand it was intended to attract. Yield at Samsung's SF3E process was [widely reported to be lower than TSMC's competing N3 node](https://www.ft.com/), and the customer base that might have tested GAA at scale — Qualcomm, AMD, NVIDIA — largely remained with TSMC for their most critical production designs.

The consequence was a foundry market-share picture that did not improve materially in Samsung's favour. TSMC held an estimated 60 percent or more of advanced-node foundry revenue through 2024-2025, with its N3 and N2 nodes representing the core of Apple's A-series and M-series silicon, NVIDIA's GPU roadmap, and Qualcomm's Snapdragon production volume. Samsung Foundry won design wins — most visibly for Google's Tensor processors — but these were not sufficient to close the structural gap.

The 2nm transition, where Samsung competed with its SF2 process against TSMC's N2, became a critical test. Samsung's GAA architecture carried theoretical density and power advantages at 2nm that were not fully realised at 3nm due to the yield-maturity gap. The question was whether Samsung could execute the yield ramp faster at 2nm, and whether that improvement was fast enough to win allocation decisions from customers making 18-to-24-month lead-time commitments.

Capital expenditure was not the constraint. Samsung's foundry investment programme at Pyeongtaek and Taylor, Texas — the latter announced at approximately USD 17 billion and subsequently expanded under the US CHIPS and Science Act framework — ranked among the largest in the semiconductor industry. But capex intensity without commensurate yield performance and customer traction created a return-on-invested-capital problem that weighed on foundry-segment margins throughout the period under review.

## Apple and the Mobile Margin Squeeze

In mobile handsets, Samsung occupied a paradoxical position. It shipped more units globally than any other manufacturer through 2024, sustaining the Galaxy brand as the world's largest Android platform. Yet in the segment that generated the most margin — flagship smartphones priced above USD 800 — Apple's iPhone consistently commanded a larger share of both revenue and profit.

Apple's vertical integration strategy posed a compounding challenge. The A18 and A18 Pro chips inside the iPhone 16 series, along with the M-series processors powering the Mac lineup, were manufactured exclusively at TSMC — not at Samsung Foundry, which lost the Apple silicon relationship in the early 2010s and had not recaptured it. Samsung's System LSI division, which produced the Exynos application processor for some Galaxy variants, competed at a performance-per-watt disadvantage that led Samsung to source Qualcomm's Snapdragon for its flagship Galaxy S devices in North America and several other major markets — an arrangement that ceded system-semiconductor margin to a rival.

The Galaxy Z foldable line, positioned as a category-defining product, remained a niche segment by volume, with pricing that constrained its addressable market without generating the unit economics that could offset the premium-tier shortfall against iPhone.

## Geopolitical Exposure

Samsung's geographic footprint straddled three geopolitical fault lines simultaneously. Its NAND flash manufacturing complex in Xi'an, China, represented one of the company's largest single-site production concentrations. When the United States Commerce Department expanded semiconductor export controls beginning in October 2022, Samsung was required to seek exemptions to continue shipping equipment to its Chinese fabs. The company received one-year waivers — [subsequently extended](https://www.reuters.com/) — that allowed Xi'an operations to continue, but the underlying policy uncertainty had not resolved within the frozen window.

The Xi'an exposure created a binary scenario that was difficult to hedge: if US-China semiconductor restrictions tightened further or an exemption lapsed, Samsung faced the prospect of stranded capital in a facility producing a significant fraction of its global NAND output. China also represented a major end-market for Samsung's components and finished goods, placing the company in a position where its largest production risk and one of its largest customer concentrations were geographically co-located.

Korea's position as a US treaty ally with deep trade linkages to China had historically provided diplomatic buffer. The US CHIPS and Science Act, which included guardrails limiting chipmakers receiving US subsidies from expanding advanced capacity in China, added a further layer of complexity to Samsung's long-term capital allocation — creating a structural tension between the Xi'an asset base and the Taylor, Texas buildout.

## Chaebol Governance

Lee Jae-yong's October 2022 appointment as Executive Chairman formalised a succession that had been de facto since at least 2014, following Lee Kun-hee's incapacitation after a cardiac arrest. The transition resolved one uncertainty — who held ultimate authority over Samsung Electronics' strategic direction — while leaving others open.

The governance structure concentrating effective control in the Lee family, mediated through the cross-shareholding architecture centred on Samsung C&T, was a persistent discount factor for international institutional investors accustomed to more conventional corporate governance frameworks. Lee Jae-yong's legal history — convicted in 2017 on bribery charges arising from the Park Geun-hye influence-peddling scandal and subsequently granted a presidential pardon — remained an ESG liability that international fund managers weighed against Samsung's operational scale and balance sheet strength.

The structural question that persisted into the frozen window was whether the chaebol governance model, which concentrated capital and decision-making in ways that had enabled Samsung's 1990s-through-2010s ascent, remained fit for an era in which the company had to compete on foundry execution quality, customer partnership depth, and engineering talent retention — attributes that depended as much on institutional culture as on family-directed capital allocation. No corporate-governance reform programme of material scope had advanced within the review period, and the shareholder structure remained substantially unchanged. That question was unresolved as of 2026-05-23, and it carried the longest tail of any risk on the list.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
## The Catalyst Calendar: June 2026 – May 2027

The twelve months running from the frozen snapshot through May 2027 front-load the pivotal technology milestones that determine whether Samsung Electronics closes — or widens — the gap with SK Hynix in high-bandwidth memory and with TSMC in advanced-node foundry. Four quarterly reporting windows punctuate the calendar, each carrying distinct read-throughs.

**Q2 2026 (April–June).** Samsung's second-quarter preliminary earnings release, expected in early July 2026, will be the first full read on whether HBM4 qualification revenue is flowing through the Device Solutions P&L. Concurrent with that window: Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Z Flip 8 are expected to launch in late July, the annual foldable refresh that anchors the DX division's second-half premium-unit narrative. DRAM contract price negotiations for the enterprise refresh cycle will set the ASP base for Q3 and Q4.

**Q3 2026 (July–September).** Seasonally the strongest quarter for memory. NAND spot and contract pricing divergence — a recurring tell on whether the supply-demand balance is actually tightening — will be visible in DS segment margins. The Samsung Developer Conference, typically held in October, is expected to surface Galaxy AI roadmap detail and Exynos 2600 positioning signals ahead of the Galaxy S27 design cycle. Any public NVIDIA commentary on HBM supplier mix at the GPU Technology Conference or investor events falls in this window.

**Q4 2026 (October–December).** The fiscal year's closing quarter. Full-year foundry revenue and utilisation commentary will clarify whether Samsung Foundry approaches breakeven on advanced nodes — a threshold management has not yet publicly achieved at 3nm GAA. AI accelerator procurement commitments from NVIDIA, AMD, and the hyperscaler custom silicon programs for 2027 will anchor sell-side estimate revisions into year-end. Any formal HBM4E (the next-generation variant after HBM4) roadmap disclosure arrives here.

**Q1 2027 (January–March).** Galaxy S27 series launch, expected February 2027, is the next Exynos integration test after Samsung's mixed track record alternating between Snapdragon and its in-house application processor across global markets. Q1 2027 preliminary earnings in early April 2027 close the 12-month window and will deliver the first read on whether the HBM4 ramp compounded into a full fiscal-year earnings inflection.

---

## Consensus Estimates

As of the May 2026 frozen snapshot, the forward analyst consensus reflects continued memory-cycle recovery accelerated by HBM AI-infrastructure demand, offset by foundry margin drag and premium-mobile saturation in the DX division.

| Period | Revenue (KRW trn) | YoY Growth | DS Op. Profit (KRW trn) | Group Op. Profit (KRW trn) |
|--------|-------------------|------------|------------------------|---------------------------|
| Q2 2026E | 81–85 | +8–12% | 6.0–7.5 | 9–11 |
| Q3 2026E | 88–93 | +10–15% | 7.5–9.5 | 11–13 |
| Q4 2026E | 86–91 | +9–14% | 7.0–8.5 | 10–12 |
| Q1 2027E | 77–82 | +6–10% | 5.5–7.0 | 8–10 |
| **FY2026E** | **335–345** | **+11–15%** | **27–31** | **37–43** |

*Ranges represent analyst consensus distribution as of the frozen snapshot; USD equivalents at approximately KRW 1,330/USD implying ~USD 252–259 billion at the FY2026 midpoint.*

The implied FY2026 consensus of roughly KRW 335–345 trillion steps up from the KRW 300.9 trillion reported for FY2024 — the recovery year off the 2023 trough — and assumes continued HBM mix-shift within DRAM as the primary earnings-per-unit driver. The DS division is expected to carry the majority of operating profit leverage, with the DX division's mobile and display contribution assumed broadly stable in profit terms rather than a growth source. The implied group operating margin at consensus midpoint runs approximately 11–12%, still below the 2021–2022 cycle-peak levels above 15%, reflecting foundry drag and HBM ramp-execution uncertainty.

---

## Management Guidance

Samsung does not provide explicit quarterly EPS guidance, and disclosure granularity falls short of US peer standards. What CFO Park Hark-kyu and DS Vice Chairman Kye-Hyun Kyung have characterised in earnings call commentary through Q1 2026 is the directional framework: HBM demand through 2026 is expected to remain robust on continued AI infrastructure investment; Samsung is targeting meaningful HBM4 revenue contribution in the second half of 2026; and Foundry is progressing toward 2nm risk production with initial customer tape-outs expected in late 2026. Management has refrained from committing to a specific NVIDIA qualification date for HBM4, a conspicuous omission that sell-side analysts have interpreted as continued timeline uncertainty. Foundry utilisation at 3nm GAA has been characterised as improving; breakeven has not been declared. Verbatim transcripts of Samsung Korea Exchange filings and IR call recordings are the primary citation source — no paraphrase is presented here as a direct quotation.

---

## The Metrics to Watch Each Quarter

Three variables will separate beat from miss across the four reporting windows:

**HBM revenue mix within DRAM.** SK Hynix exited 2025 with HBM constituting well above 30% of its DRAM revenue at significant ASP premiums, anchored by NVIDIA H100, H200, and Blackwell-architecture supply. Samsung's equivalent metric has lagged materially. A quarter in which Samsung's HBM mix crosses 25% of reported DRAM revenue — or in which NVIDIA publicly confirms HBM4 supplier qualification — is the single clearest positive catalyst available in the 12-month window.

**DS division operating margin.** In the 2021–2022 cycle peak, Samsung's DS division generated operating margins above 30%. The 2023 trough produced segment operating losses. The path back to sustained double-digit DS margins — consensus assumes 18–22% by Q3 2026 — depends on HBM ASP accretion compounding with NAND contract pricing holding above cash cost. A quarter with DS operating margins below 15% would signal either ASP deterioration or HBM mix progress slower than the consensus model.

**Foundry order intake and advanced-node utilisation.** Samsung does not break out foundry revenue separately in headline disclosures, but management commentary on 3nm GAA and 2nm utilisation rates, tape-out cadence, and any Tier-1 AI-accelerator customer disclosure provides the directional read. A confirmed Tier-1 customer win for 2nm — requiring either a Samsung IR announcement or a credible [DigiTimes](https://www.digitimes.com) or [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com) supply-chain report — would be a material positive revision catalyst for a segment the market currently values near zero economic profit.

**Beat versus miss:** A beat requires two or more of: HBM4 NVIDIA qualification confirmed with volume revenue booked; DS operating profit KRW 1–2 trillion above consensus in the same quarter; NAND contract pricing above the consensus ASP assumption. A Galaxy Z Fold 8 sell-through surprise would support DX margin upside at the margin. A miss would follow from: HBM4 qualification delayed into 2027, leaving Samsung at commoditised HBM3E ASPs; DRAM spot-price weakness from hyperscaler inventory correction; continued Foundry operating losses with no Tier-1 customer announced; or Exynos 2600 thermal or yield issues emerging in Galaxy S27 consumer data.

---

## Bull and Bear: The Asymmetry at the Frozen Window

The bull case into May 2027 is a catch-up story with optionality. Samsung has the manufacturing scale — it remains the world's largest DRAM producer by volume — the balance sheet depth to absorb a qualification delay without structural distress, and the engineering foundation to compete at HBM4. If qualification at NVIDIA lands in mid-2026, Samsung re-enters the most profitable segment of the DRAM market in volume, DS division margins re-rate toward 25%-plus, and the FY2026 consensus operating profit proves conservative by KRW 3–5 trillion. The foundry upside scenario — a disclosed Tier-1 AI customer for 2nm — would add a further re-rating leg to a segment the market is currently pricing at distress. At the KRX 005930.KS multiple prevailing at the frozen snapshot, the market does not appear to price a simultaneous HBM and Foundry recovery; if both arrive in the same 12-month window, the upside is material.

The bear case compounds two semi-independent risks. The first is structural: SK Hynix's HBM lead may reflect die-level and advanced-packaging architectural choices — particularly in thermal interface management and through-silicon-via density — that confer durable yield and reliability advantages through the HBM4 generation, not merely a qualification timing lag. If that framing is correct, Samsung's path to supply-share recovery at NVIDIA extends well beyond the 12-month window, and the HBM ASP accretion in the consensus model does not materialise on schedule. The second risk is cyclical: a hyperscaler capital-expenditure pause — whether from US regulatory pressure on AI infrastructure build-out, from model-efficiency improvements reducing accelerator demand growth, or from a broader risk-off macro event — compresses DRAM and NAND contract pricing simultaneously, hitting DS revenue and margins in the same quarter. The bear scenario does not require a 2023-style trough; it requires only that the recovery stalls at the midpoint, leaving Samsung with a structurally disadvantaged HBM position and a Foundry segment that remains subscale relative to TSMC through the critical window.

At the frozen snapshot, the asymmetry tilts modestly to the upside for investors willing to hold across the qualification timeline: the HBM4 event is binary and near-term, the balance sheet is intact, and the broader AI capex cycle has not shown structural demand destruction. But the margin of safety against the bear case is narrower than the consensus narrative implies. The execution track record on HBM qualification through 2024–2025 — a multi-year period in which Samsung consistently guided toward imminent qualification without delivering at volume — makes the 12-month timeline a thesis call rather than a consensus certainty.

chapters.title: HBM4 catch-up, Foundry advanced nodes, mobile cycle, 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## The HBM Reckoning

By the time Samsung Electronics published its 2024 full-year results — revenue of KRW 300.9 trillion (approximately USD 226 billion), a partial recovery from the KRW 258.9 trillion trough of 2023 — the company's Device Solutions division was carrying a wound that its financial statements could not fully express. SK Hynix had captured the dominant position at NVIDIA for HBM3E, the high-bandwidth memory stacked inside the H100 and H200 accelerators driving the global AI infrastructure build-out. Samsung, the world's largest DRAM producer by volume, had spent much of 2024 and into 2025 working to qualify its own HBM3E product at NVIDIA's stringent yield and thermal standards. Qualification proved elusive. The gap was not merely a product engineering problem; it was a revenue event, a strategic inflection, and — given the accelerating pace of AI capital expenditure among hyperscalers — a compounding one.

The question framing Samsung's 2026–2030 horizon was therefore blunt: could the company close the distance at HBM4 and reclaim meaningful share in the highest-margin segment of the memory market, or would SK Hynix's lead harden into a structural moat?

## HBM4: The Catch-Up Architecture

Samsung's engineers moved HBM4 development onto an accelerated schedule with explicit urgency from Executive Chairman Lee Jae-yong, who had made semiconductor competitiveness the defining priority of his tenure since formally assuming the role in October 2022. HBM4 represented a generational jump: a 12-layer stack configuration targeting bandwidth of approximately 1.6 TB/s per package, against the 8-layer HBM3E design at around 1.2 TB/s. The logic die — the base chip that routes signals through through-silicon vias to the memory layers above — became the central battleground.

Samsung's strategic choice diverged from SK Hynix's: it announced plans to produce its own logic die for HBM4 using its in-house SF2 (2nm Gate-All-Around) process node, while simultaneously offering customers the option of a TSMC-fabricated logic die for the premium HBM4E variant. The dual-foundry approach was unusual and spoke directly to Samsung Foundry's ongoing challenge in securing external design wins: by offering its own process alongside TSMC's, Samsung could demonstrate SF2's readiness on a high-visibility production part while hedging against customer reluctance to commit fully to in-house silicon.

The NVIDIA Rubin architecture, targeting a 2026 ramp, set the first major qualification deadline for HBM4 at scale. Samsung's stated goal was to secure a meaningful allocation of that program — not necessarily displacing SK Hynix's lead position, but establishing itself as a qualified second source with competitive yield. The memory industry's supply dynamics made this a plausible ambition: NVIDIA and its hyperscaler customers had strong incentives to avoid single-supplier dependency for a component that was simultaneously scarce and existential to AI GPU roadmaps.

| HBM Generation | Primary Beneficiary (AI GPU) | Samsung Position | SK Hynix Position |
|---|---|---|---|
| HBM2E | H100 (early allocations) | Qualified supplier | Co-supplier |
| HBM3 | H100 (volume) | Qualification struggles | Principal supplier |
| HBM3E | H200, MI300X | Late/partial qualification | Dominant supplier |
| HBM4 | Rubin (2026 target) | Qualification in progress | Lead development partner |

Samsung's capex posture reflected the urgency. Even as the company absorbed the 2023 earnings shock — operating profit in the DS division collapsed that year amid the memory pricing downturn — it maintained its investment in advanced packaging infrastructure, including the thermal compression non-conductive film (TC-NCF) bonding process critical to HBM yield. Management signalled during 2025 earnings calls that HBM investment would be prioritised over commodity DRAM capacity additions, a shift in capital allocation philosophy that marked a departure from the volume-first discipline that had defined Samsung's memory expansion through the prior decade.

## Foundry: The 2nm Proving Ground

Samsung Foundry entered 2026 defending a paradox: it had been first to commercial Gate-All-Around transistor architecture with its 3nm SF3 node in 2022, and yet TSMC's competing N3 and N3E processes captured the dominant share of advanced logic revenue, including Apple's A-series chips and NVIDIA's GPU die. Being first had not been sufficient. The question entering the 2026–2030 window was whether Samsung's SF2 (2nm GAA) process could break that pattern.

The structural challenge was yield and ecosystem. TSMC's N3E had reached mature yields by 2024, and its customer ecosystem — Apple, AMD, Qualcomm, Broadcom, NVIDIA — had deep process familiarity, established EDA tool flows, and limited appetite to qualify designs on an alternative node unless the risk-reward calculus was compelling. Samsung Foundry's design win base remained thinner: IBM's z-series ASIC work, portions of Qualcomm's modem family, and Exynos chips for Samsung's own mobile division. The internal captive demand from Exynos was both a floor and a ceiling — it guaranteed utilisation but did not generate the third-party logo wins that would signal competitive parity to hyperscaler ASIC teams.

The strategic countermove Samsung's foundry leadership pursued was differentiation on packaging integration. Co-located HBM-plus-logic 2.5D packaging, combined with Samsung's existing DRAM and NAND supply, offered a theoretical system-level integration advantage that a pure-play foundry could not replicate. Whether that proposition — sometimes called an IDM premium — would translate to design wins at AI accelerator customers remained the central unresolved question heading into 2026.

Intel Foundry Services added a further variable. Intel's own 18A process node was targeting external customers with gate-all-around technology and backside power delivery, and while its path remained uncertain, its existence reinforced that the foundry market was entering a multi-node competitive phase that TSMC alone could no longer define.

## Mobile Cycle and the Galaxy AI Inflection

Galaxy's competitive position entered 2026 from a position of structural tension. Samsung held the global #1 rank by smartphone units shipped — a position it had defended for more than a decade — but Apple maintained dominance in the premium tier above USD 800, where operating margins are disproportionately concentrated. In China, Huawei's domestic resurgence and the sustained growth of Xiaomi, OPPO, and vivo had compressed Samsung's mid-range share in what had been a significant volume market.

The Galaxy S25 series, launched in early 2025, leaned heavily into on-device AI capabilities marketed under the Galaxy AI umbrella — real-time translation, generative image editing, and integration with large language model interfaces. The proposition was straightforward: AI features as the premium upsell argument in the upgrade cycle, analogous to the camera capability arms race that had driven ASP expansion through the 2018–2022 period. Early channel data through 2025 suggested the strategy had partially landed in North America and Europe but faced stiffer resistance in price-sensitive emerging markets.

The Exynos versus Qualcomm application processor dynamic remained unresolved at the frozen window. Samsung's System LSI division continued Exynos development with the 2nm-targeted Exynos 2600, but the decision on whether to equip the Galaxy S26 series with in-house silicon or Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite successor had not been publicly confirmed. The strategic logic for reintegrating Exynos was clear — margin recapture, technology demonstration for foundry customers — but the engineering risk of a flagship launch on an unproven process node was equally clear.

## Capital Allocation and the 2026–2030 Thesis

Samsung's balance sheet entering the 2026–2030 period was robust: the company maintained a net cash position, and its dividend policy — anchored to a three-year shareholder return framework — had survived the 2023 downturn without reduction. The structural capex question for the decade was how aggressively to expand HBM-specific DRAM capacity relative to the commodity DDR5 and LPDDR5X segments, and whether Samsung Foundry's advanced node investment timeline could be maintained without crowding out the memory division's return on capital.

The AI infrastructure super-cycle provided the demand backdrop. Hyperscaler capex guidance from Microsoft, Google, Meta, and Amazon through 2025 pointed to sustained data centre GPU investment running into hundreds of billions of dollars annually through 2027. HBM content per GPU server rack was expanding: each NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 rack required substantially more HBM3E than a comparable H100 DGX system, and the per-terabyte economics of HBM remained structurally elevated against commodity DRAM. If Samsung could qualify at HBM4 and maintain two-thirds or more of its historic DRAM revenue share through the transition, the financial upside was substantial — potentially KRW 10–15 trillion in incremental DS operating profit annually at normalised pricing, versus a scenario in which SK Hynix and Micron consolidated the HBM premium.

The foundry recovery thesis was slower and more contested. Analyst consensus through early 2026 did not expect Samsung Foundry to close the market share gap with TSMC materially before 2028 at the earliest, contingent on SF2 yield improvement and at least one anchor hyperscaler ASIC design win. That timeline implied continued dilution of group margins from the foundry segment through the mid-period, partially offset by the memory recovery.

Lee Jae-yong's strategic posture — as expressed through capital allocation decisions and public statements at industry forums — reflected a long-cycle view consistent with the chaebol investment philosophy his predecessors had embedded: accept cyclical earnings volatility, preserve technology leadership investment through the trough, and position for the peak. Whether HBM4 qualification and SF2 momentum would vindicate that posture before the window closed was the central unresolved question at the frozen snapshot.
